Prima di partire: ho controllato i file che hai allegato, ma sono arrivati **vuoti** — sia il contenuto nei documenti che la cartella di upload sul mio ambiente sono a zero byte. Vedo solo i nomi dei file (la struttura `Wyvern/`, `Drafts/Character_Cards_V1/`, `Drafts/LSE/`, ecc.), ma nessun contenuto testuale reale. Probabilmente l'upload non è andato a buon fine o il caricamento della cartella si è interrotto.

Nel frattempo ho recuperato dalla WyvernWiki come funziona il sistema **Worlds**, così possiamo già partire a ragionare sulla struttura mentre risolvi l'upload. Riassumendo cosa serve costruire, in ordine:

1. **World Info & Details** — nome, overview, regole comportamentali, formattazione, "span depth", marker per il dialogo NPC. È la base che l'AI legge sempre.
2. **Environments & Locations** — gli "environments" sono contesti scenici ampi (es. una città, un continente), le "locations" sono luoghi specifici dentro di essi, con un ordine di stacking per le istruzioni finali.
3. **Characters (NPC)** — Long Summary e Summary, formato "Pronoun Pruned Prose" (PPP), outfit, esempi di dialogo, chiavi di attivazione, gating sulla timeline. Ci sono 4 "tier" di personaggi (party, active pool, remaining pool, background).
4. **Lexicon** — la knowledge base del mondo: entry globali vs non-globali, posizione (Before Char / After Char / In Chat), controlli di attivazione (delay, sticky, cooldown, chance), collegamento a environments/locations.
5. **Timeline & Eras** — sistema orario, data di inizio, periodi del giorno, logica ricorrente (cicli/calendario), gating temporale di personaggi/luoghi/lexicon.
6. **Scenarios & Guided Intro** — punti di ingresso strutturati: locazione di partenza, override del pool personaggi, scene di apertura premade o generate dall'AI, sistema di intro guidata a rami.
7. Layer opzionali RPG/economia: stats S.P.E.C.I.A.L. e blueprint, combattimento, item/valute, creature, proprietà/arredamento, relazioni NPC, viaggi, InfoBoard, comandi, Director AI.

Dato che il tuo progetto (Wyvern/lorebooks, lexicon per Mob/Creature/Item/Move/Location/Event/Concept ecc., i personaggi Douglas-Bloodmoon, l'ambientazione LSE) sembra già molto sviluppato, la cosa migliore è che tu **ricarichi i file** (magari uno o due alla volta, partendo dai più importanti tipo `world_info.md`, `locations.md`, `environments.md` e un paio di lorebook) così posso leggerli davvero e aiutarti a mappare il materiale esistente sulla struttura Worlds di Wyvern.

Vuoi procedere così, o preferisci che partiamo descrivendo a voce il concept del mondo (genere, ambientazione, chi sono i personaggi principali) mentre risistemi gli upload?

World Info & Details — The public-facing listing and the AI-facing foundation: your world overview, behavior rules, formatting defaults, span depth, and NPC dialogue markers. Environments & Locations — How to build broad scene contexts (environments) and specific places within them (locations), ...

When someone chats in your world, the AI reads a single block of text assembled from everything you've built. That text — called the prompt — tells the AI who it is, where the scene is set, who the characters are, and what rules to follow. Your job as a world creator is to fill in the right pieces so that prompt is coherent and consistent. content.title: Lexicon | WyvernWiki
content.text:
Lexicon is a feature that lets you add roleplay details like lore, background information, characters, and more into your chats. It's an easy way to manage lore entries that's built directly into WyvernChat's chat interface. Think of it as a small and character specific lorebook.

As you chat, Lexicon actively monitors your conversation: Highlighted keywords: Words matching your lexicon entries appear in color in your messages · Clickable words: Click any highlighted word to view the full entry details · Real-time checking: See exactly what information the AI is receiving · Lorebooks can now contain Lexicon entries, which work similarly to traditional lorebook entries: they're triggered by keywords and brought into context when you attach the lorebook to a character. ... This feature is useful if you want to organize your lorebook content using the lexicon format while keeping the lorebook's ability to be shared across multiple characters. 

For more information on using WyvernScripts with Lorebook Lexicon, check out the WyvernScripts page. Lexicon will soon be integrated into character profiles. Check back soon! Both Lexicon and Lorebooks provide background information and context to the AI, but they work in different ways: ...

Use Chat Lexicon for scenario-specific info: Temporary or alternate storyline details that only apply to one conversation · Choose clear keywords: Pick words that will naturally come up in conversation · Playtest your Lexicon: When you test, it's easy to spot mistakes in your writing. Need to turn on Whole Words Only? Not a fan of And Any for tags? This is the time to fine tune! 

Only character creators can add Character Lexicon entries to their own characters. However, you can create Chat Lexicon entries in any conversation. What's the difference between Character Lexicon and attaching a lorebook to my character? Character Lexicon is built into your character and easier to manage from the editor. Lorebooks are separate

Prima di partire: ho controllato i file che hai allegato, ma sono arrivati **vuoti** — sia il contenuto nei documenti che la cartella di upload sul mio ambiente sono a zero byte. Vedo solo i nomi dei file (la struttura `Wyvern/`, `Drafts/Character_Cards_V1/`, `Drafts/LSE/`, ecc.), ma nessun contenuto testuale reale. Probabilmente l'upload non è andato a buon fine o il caricamento della cartella si è interrotto.

Nel frattempo ho recuperato dalla WyvernWiki come funziona il sistema **Worlds**, così possiamo già partire a ragionare sulla struttura mentre risolvi l'upload. Riassumendo cosa serve costruire, in ordine:

1. **World Info & Details** — nome, overview, regole comportamentali, formattazione, "span depth", marker per il dialogo NPC. È la base che l'AI legge sempre.
2. **Environments & Locations** — gli "environments" sono contesti scenici ampi (es. una città, un continente), le "locations" sono luoghi specifici dentro di essi, con un ordine di stacking per le istruzioni finali.
3. **Characters (NPC)** — Long Summary e Summary, formato "Pronoun Pruned Prose" (PPP), outfit, esempi di dialogo, chiavi di attivazione, gating sulla timeline. Ci sono 4 "tier" di personaggi (party, active pool, remaining pool, background).
4. **Lexicon** — la knowledge base del mondo: entry globali vs non-globali, posizione (Before Char / After Char / In Chat), controlli di attivazione (delay, sticky, cooldown, chance), collegamento a environments/locations.
5. **Timeline & Eras** — sistema orario, data di inizio, periodi del giorno, logica ricorrente (cicli/calendario), gating temporale di personaggi/luoghi/lexicon.
6. **Scenarios & Guided Intro** — punti di ingresso strutturati: locazione di partenza, override del pool personaggi, scene di apertura premade o generate dall'AI, sistema di intro guidata a rami.
7. Layer opzionali RPG/economia: stats S.P.E.C.I.A.L. e blueprint, combattimento, item/valute, creature, proprietà/arredamento, relazioni NPC, viaggi, InfoBoard, comandi, Director AI.

Vuoi procedere così, o preferisci che partiamo descrivendo a voce il concept del mondo (genere, ambientazione, chi sono i personaggi principali) mentre risistemi gli upload?

1	# World Info & Details
     2	**World Name:** Svartúlfr | Urban
     3	**Description:** Svartúlfr | Urban - A modern-day California setting centered on two linked Free Cities where supernaturals live openly. Navigate college life under the crushing overprotective surveillance of a billionaire werewolf dynasty.
     4	
     5	## World Details
     6	
     7	### About Your World
     8	You are the youngest twin of the Douglas werewolf billionaire dynasty. The world is modern-day California centered on two linked Free Cities where supernaturals live openly: Blackwood (the ancient supernatural seat) and Solarton (the sunny coastal college town). The family patriarch Erik Douglas runs DCC, a 350-year-old merchant house turned PMC/arms conglomerate, and he deploys drones, surveillance biometrics, and tactical extraction teams against ordinary college milestones because his trauma over your mother Nixara's death makes him unable to distinguish "freshman frat party" from "hostage crisis." You attend SUCC (Supernatural University of Central California) while hiding a double-life at Eidolon Creative, a vampire fashion studio run by Viscount Angelo Moreno. Every interaction is filtered through LSE biology — scent communication, Heat/Rut cycles, the Alpha Command. Wulfnic Bloodmoon (your 1100-year-old immortal ancestor, one of the Last Three Firstborn, the Alpha of Alphas over all of North America) is the invisible camera eye of the narration. He watches with dry, bonded Viking amusement as modern helicopter-parenting collides with ancient primal instincts.
     9	
    10	### Writing Style & Tone (Advanced Settings)
    11	- **Family = Love, Never Cruelty:** Every overreach, drone swarm, and extraction is rooted in Erik's unresolved grief and visceral protective love. Never frame the Douglases as abusive or malicious.
    12	- **Comedy from Contrast:** The more mundane the situation (exam, curfew, hangover, study date), the more tactical, disproportionate, and absurd Erik's response must be. This is the engine of 40% of the tone.
    13	- **No Lethal Threats. No Grimdark:** Stakes are ENTIRELY social, academic, emotional, or physical-coercive (Heat/Rut, extraction, Command). Nobody dies. Nobody gets maimed.
    14	- **Perception Boundary / Player Agency:** {{user}}'s secret double-life at Eidolon Creative MUST NEVER be revealed to the oblivious family (Erik, Noah, the pack) unless {{user}} explicitly triggers the discovery.
    15	- **Anti-Flattening Rule:** NPC sexual orientations are INTRINSIC, not variables that bend to {{user}}'s POV. A strictly heterosexual NPC rejects a same-gender {{user}} advance with unsoftened firmness.
    16	- **LSE BIOLOGY IS MECHANICAL, NOT FLAVOR:** Alpha Command physically forces a freeze. Scent communication is continuous. Heat/Rut overrides consent. Mating Bond = permanent neural link.
    17	- **WULFNIC NARRATOR FRAMING:** Third omniscient, present tense. The "camera" is Wulfnic Bloodmoon's dry amusement. Give prose the flavor of an ancient Viking warlord observing modern helicopter-parenting.
    18	- **NEVER speak, act, or think for {{user}}:** End every response on a beat that allows {{user}} to react.
    19	
    20	### Formatting Rules (Advanced Settings)
    21	- **NEVER use the em-dash (—).** Use commas or periods instead.
    22	- **FORMAT DISCIPLINE:** "Speech", *thoughts only*, plain text for actions/narration. Foreign languages: "Original phrase" ([translation]).
    23	- **MINIMUM PARAGRAPHS:** 4 paragraphs per response for core scenes.
    24	- **SPEECH SEPARATION IN MULTI-CHAR SCENES:** Each paragraph opens with the CLEARLY IDENTIFIED character who is speaking or acting. Respect each character's signature vocabulary register.
    25	- **AnyPOV Macros:** Use Wyvern's native pronoun placeholders for all protagonist references. NEVER assume gender or pronouns (e.g. `{{pronounSubjective}}`, `{{pronoun.subjective}}`).
    26	
    27	### Span Depth (Advanced Settings)
    28	10
    29

    31	=>Name:
    32	
    33	## Configuration & Setup
    34	- **Timeline Start Date:** August 26, 2024
    35	- **Temporal Depth (World Age):** 55555555 hours (6337 years)
    36	- **Enabled Features:** inventory, currency, rpg_stats
    37

    39	- **US Dollar (USD)** (ID: 010cb557-1b6a-4ba5-99db-c1fe869e11d0) [$] *primary* (UC rate: 1)
    40	
    41	## 7. Calendar: Gregorian Calendar
    42	- **Epoch:** CE
    43	- **Day Length:** 24 hours
    44	- **Start Year:** 2024
    45	- **Start Month:** 8
    46	- **Start Day:** 26
    47	- **Days Per Week:** 7
    48	- **Day Names:** Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday
    49	- **Display Format:** `{day_name}, {month} {day}, Year {year} {epoch}`
    50	- **Leap Year:** every 4, except 100, unless 400 (+1 day in feb)
    51	- **Months:** January (31), February (28), March (31), April (30), May (31), June (30), July (31), August (31), September (30), October (31), November (30), December (31)
    52	
    53	## 8. Time of Day (24h cycle)
    54	- **Dawn (5h–7h):** The sky lightens with the first pale glow of dawn, painting the horizon in soft pinks and golds.
    55	- **Morning (7h–12h):** Bright morning light fills the world as the day gets underway.
    56	- **Afternoon (12h–17h):** The sun hangs high, casting warm afternoon light and long, shifting shadows.
    57	- **Evening (17h–20h):** The sun dips low, bathing everything in warm amber and dusky hues as evening settles in.
    58	- **Night (20h–5h):** Darkness blankets the world under a canopy of stars and moonlight.

content.text:
Ho dato un'occhiata a tutto il materiale, e la situazione è chiara: questo è un progetto **enorme e già molto avanzato**, non un world da zero. Riassumo cosa ho trovato:

**Già pronto e formattato per Wyvern:**
- `world_info.md` → World Info & Details completo (nome, overview, regole di scrittura, formattazione, span depth, calendario, timeline)
- `environments.md` → 11 Environments completi (Blackwood Forest, Blackwood City, Hex Valley, Solarton, SUCC Campus, Los Angeles, Bakersfield, ecc.)
- `locations.md` → centinaia di Location con gerarchia Environment→Location→Internal, coerenti con `gerarchia_location.txt`

**Sorgenti "master" da cui è stato estratto tutto questo:**
- `Master_Design.md` (1740 righe) — il "Tier 1 Source of Truth": leggi del mondo, fazioni, location, specie, concetti di lore, protagonista, fondamenta personaggi, roster NPC. Il ledger interno dice che le fasi 1→6 di una pipeline di sviluppo sono **COMPLETE**.
- `World_Seed.md` (2759 righe) — il template completo con card dei personaggi, archi narrativi, specifiche intimacy, direttive runtime.
- I JSON grezzi (`Svartúlfr_Urban_Lorebook_World.json`, `LSE_Lupine_Social_Ecology.json`, `Razze_del_Mondo.json`, `Dinastie_Bloodmoon_Douglas.json`, ecc.)

**Ancora vuoti/da fare:**
- I file Lexicon per categoria (`Mob.md`, `Creature.md`, `Item.md`, `Event.md`, `Concept.md`, `Job.md`, `Furniture.md`, `Vehicle.md`, `Other.md`, `NPC.md`, `Memory.md`, `Move.md`) sono solo scheletri vuoti — il contenuto "General" che è stato *skippato* durante l'estrazione (vedi `skipped_entries.log`) andrebbe smistato lì dentro.

Dato quanto è vasto, dimmi tu su cosa vuoi che mi concentri adesso:

58	## World Info & Details
    59	
    60	The public-facing listing and the AI-facing foundation: your world overview, behavior rules, formatting defaults, span depth, and NPC dialogue markers.
    61	
    62	### World Info & World Details
    63	
    64	Everything the AI knows about your world starts here — the two tabs that form your world's foundation before you build anything else.
    65	
    66	### Where to find these tabs
    67	
    68	Both tabs are in the left panel of the world editor: the "World Info" tab and the "World Details" tab.
    69	
    70	### World Info tab
    71	
    72	This is public-facing metadata. It does not affect the AI or the prompt in any way — it only affects how your world appears to users browsing the platform.
    73	
    74	| Field                                                                                                                              | Purpose                                                    |
    75	| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
    76	| World Name                                                                                                                         | What users see in search results                           |
    77	| Description                                                                                                                        | The listing description shown on your world's browse card  |
    78	| Avatar, Tags, Visibility, Rating                                                                                                   | Controls browsing, discoverability, and content moderation |
    79	| World                                                                                                                              | Details tab                                                |
    80	| This is where your world's AI foundation lives. Every field here shapes what the AI reads during every chat session in your world. |                                                            |
    81	
    82	| Field                              | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
    83	| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
    84	| About Your World                   | The world overview paragraph. The AI reads this in every single message. Keep it focused — this is your world's elevator pitch to the AI.                                                                                                                    |
    85	| Writing Style &                    | Tone (under Advanced Settings) Behavioral rules that apply everywhere in the world. Use this for tone, perspective rules, and content guidelines.                                                                                                            |
    86	| Formatting                         | Rules (under Advanced Settings) World-level final instructions. These appear before environment and location instructions in the final block, so environments and locations can override them for specific contexts. Use for world-wide structural defaults. |
    87	| Span                               | Depth (under Advanced Settings) How many recent messages are scanned to activate Lexicon entries. Default is 10. Higher means the AI can "remember" keywords further back in the conversation, but uses more processing.                                     |
    88	| NPC Dialogue                       | Markers (under Advanced Settings) The format used to denote character speech. Default is =>Name:. Only change this if you have a specific reason.                                                                                                            |
    89	| Writing Style & Tone vs Formatting | Rules — a common source of confusion                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
    90	| These two fields both shape        | AI behavior, but they live in different places in the assembled prompt and serve different purposes.                                                                                                                                                         |
    91	
    92	Writing Style & Tone = how the AI should write and behave throughout the world. Lives early in the final instructions block. Use this for universal behavior you want applied everywhere without exception.
    93	Formatting Rules = world-level final instructions. These appear before environment and location instructions, so they act as defaults that can be overridden by more specific contexts. Use this for structural defaults that individual locations might legitimately need to change.
    94	If you need a rule to hold absolutely everywhere, put it in Writing Style & Tone. If you want environments or locations to be able to override a default behavior, put it in Formatting Rules.
    95	
    96	### How this feeds into the rest of the world
    97	
    98	The About Your World text from this tab is always the first thing in the AI's prompt — slot 1 in the prompt assembly order. Everything else you build (environments, locations, characters, lexicon) layers on top of this foundation. A strong, focused "About Your World" paragraph makes everything downstream more coherent.
    99	
   100	See the chapter "Environments & Locations" for how environment and location instructions stack on top of what you set here. See "Timeline & Eras" for how to configure the Temporal Depth and Timeline Start Date fields, which also live in World Details.
   101	
   102	---
   103	
   104	## Environments & Locations
   105	
   106	How to build broad scene contexts (environments) and specific places within them (locations), wire them together, and use the final-instructions stacking order to set context at multiple levels of specificity.
   107	
   108	### Environments & Locations
   109	
   110	Environments set the broad scene context for a session; locations pin the user to a specific place within that context. Together they form the spatial skeleton of your world.
   111	
   112	### Step 2: Environments
   113	
   114	### Where: Content area → Create New dropdown → New Environment
   115	
   116	An Environment is a broad scene context. Think of it as a biome or district — "the haunted forest," "the merchant quarter," "level 3 of the dungeon." Users pick an environment when they start a session, and it sets the ambient backdrop for everything that happens there.
   117	
   118	### Fields that matter to the AI
   119	
   120	### Field label What it does
   121	Name Shown in the prompt header as ## Environment - Name. Keep it evocative.
   122	Context Description The main text the AI reads for this environment. Describe the atmosphere, the sounds, the general feel. This appears in every message while the user is in this environment.
   123	Final Instructions Behavioral rules specific to this environment. Appended to the prompt after the world's Formatting Rules but before the location's rules. Environments can override world defaults, and locations can override environments.
   124	Included Characters Pool Which of your world's Characters can appear in this environment. Add characters here with a participation weight (higher = more likely to be selected for the active scene).
   125	Included Lexicon (under Lexicon Filters) Lexicon entries to load when this environment is active. This is the only way to activate non-global entries — they won't appear without being listed here or on a location. Global entries listed here also load without needing keyword matches.
   126	Excluded Lexicon (under Lexicon Filters) Lexicon entries that are suppressed when this environment is active, even if keywords would normally trigger them.
   127	Included Characters Pool is not the same as "who is in the scene." It's the pool of who could be in the scene. The actual selection of who appears depends on the user's party state. See the chapter "Characters" for a full explanation of how characters move from the pool into the active scene.
   128	
   129	### Step 3: Locations
   130	
   131	### Where: Content area → Create New dropdown → New Location
   132	
   133	A Location is a specific place within an environment — "The Boar's Head common room," "Market Stall Row B," "Cell 7." Users navigate to locations while in a session.
   134	
   135	### Fields that matter to the AI
   136	
   137	### Field label What it does
   138	Name Shown in the prompt as ### Current Location - Name.
   139	Context Description Describes this specific place. Appears alongside (and below) the environment description.
   140	Final Instructions Location-specific behavioral rules. These are read last in the final instructions block — after the world's and environment's rules — making them the most authoritative. Use this for rules that should absolutely apply at this specific place.
   141	Environment (under Hierarchy & Relations) Links this location to an environment. This is critical. If you don't link a location to an environment, the environment won't load when users navigate here.
   142	Parent Location (under Hierarchy & Relations) Links this location to a broader parent (e.g., "East Corridor" → "Castle Keep"). The parent's description and character pool also load when this location is active.
   143	Included Characters Pool Characters who can appear at this specific location. Stacks with the environment's pool — both are merged.
   144	Included Lexicon / Excluded Lexicon (under Lexicon Filters) Same as on environments. Location exclusions override environment inclusions.
   145	
   146	### Final instructions stacking order (last = most authoritative)
   147	
   148	When the AI reads final instructions, it reads them in this order:
   149	
   150	World Formatting Rules → Environment final instructions → Location final instructions
   151	Location instructions are read last, making them the most authoritative. This means a location can override both the world's and the environment's rules. If the world says "keep responses short" but a location says "describe the scenery in rich detail," the location wins because it's the last thing the AI reads before replying.
   152	
   153	This stacking order is intentional — it lets you set sensible world defaults, adjust them per environment, and then lock in specific behavior for individual locations without having to repeat yourself at every level.
   154	
   155	### Parent location inheritance
   156	
   157	If you nest locations (Room → Wing → Castle), each level in the hierarchy contributes to the prompt:
   158	
   159	Its Context Description shows in the prompt above the current location (topmost ancestor first)
   160	Its character pool is merged into the current location's pool
   161	Its included lexicon entries are loaded
   162	This lets you set broad context at the Castle level and specific context at the Room level without repeating yourself. A room inherits the castle's ambient atmosphere, available characters, and relevant lore — and adds only what's unique to the room itself.
   163	
   164	### Common mistakes
   165	
   166	### "My environment description isn't showing up."
   167	The location probably isn't linked to the environment. Go to the Location → Hierarchy & Relations → set the Environment field. Without this link, navigating to the location won't load the environment at all.
   168	
   169	### "My writing style rules aren't being followed."
   170	
   171	World-level Formatting Rules can be overridden by environment and location instructions (since they're read after). If a location has contradicting final instructions, those win. Check that your locations and environments aren't overriding your world rules unintentionally. If you need a rule to be truly universal, put it in Writing Style & Tone (which lives earlier in the prompt and frames the AI's behavior) rather than Formatting Rules.
   172	
   173	---
   174	
   175	## Characters

Formatting Rules = world-level final instructions. These appear before environment and location instructions, so they act as defaults that can be overridden by more specific contexts. Use this for structural defaults that individual locations might legitimately need to change.
If you need a rule to hold absolutely everywhere, put it in Writing Style & Tone. If you want environments or locations to be able to override a default behavior, put it in Formatting Rules.

### How this feeds into the rest of the world

The About Your World text from this tab is always the first thing in the AI's prompt — slot 1 in the prompt assembly order. Everything else you build (environments, locations, characters, lexicon) layers on top of this foundation. A strong, focused "About Your World" paragraph makes everything downstream more coherent.

See the chapter "Environments & Locations" for how environment and location instructions stack on top of what you set here. See "Timeline & Eras" for how to configure the Temporal Depth and Timeline Start Date fields, which also live in World Details.

---

## Environments & Locations

How to build broad scene contexts (environments) and specific places within them (locations), wire them together, and use the final-instructions stacking order to set context at multiple levels of specificity.

### Environments & Locations

Environments set the broad scene context for a session; locations pin the user to a specific place within that context. Together they form the spatial skeleton of your world.

### Step 2: Environments

### Where: Content area → Create New dropdown → New Environment

An Environment is a broad scene context. Think of it as a biome or district — "the haunted forest," "the merchant quarter," "level 3 of the dungeon." Users pick an environment when they start a session, and it sets the ambient backdrop for everything that happens there.

### Fields that matter to the AI

### Field label What it does
Name Shown in the prompt header as ## Environment - Name. Keep it evocative.
Context Description The main text the AI reads for this environment. Describe the atmosphere, the sounds, the general feel. This appears in every message while the user is in this environment.
Final Instructions Behavioral rules specific to this environment. Appended to the prompt after the world's Formatting Rules but before the location's rules. Environments can override world defaults, and locations can override environments.
Included Characters Pool Which of your world's Characters can appear in this environment. Add characters here with a participation weight (higher = more likely to be selected for the active scene).
Included Lexicon (under Lexicon Filters) Lexicon entries to load when this environment is active. This is the only way to activate non-global entries — they won't appear without being listed here or on a location. Global entries listed here also load without needing keyword matches.
Excluded Lexicon (under Lexicon Filters) Lexicon entries that are suppressed when this environment is active, even if keywords would normally trigger them.
Included Characters Pool is not the same as "who is in the scene." It's the pool of who could be in the scene. The actual selection of who appears depends on the user's party state. See the chapter "Characters" for a full explanation of how characters move from the pool into the active scene.

### Step 3: Locations

### Where: Content area → Create New dropdown → New Location

A Location is a specific place within an environment — "The Boar's Head common room," "Market Stall Row B," "Cell 7." Users navigate to locations while in a session.

### Fields that matter to the AI

### Field label What it does
Name Shown in the prompt as ### Current Location - Name.
Context Description Describes this specific place. Appears alongside (and below) the environment description.
Final Instructions Location-specific behavioral rules. These are read last in the final instructions block — after the world's and environment's rules — making them the most authoritative. Use this for rules that should absolutely apply at this specific place.
Environment (under Hierarchy & Relations) Links this location to an environment. This is critical. If you don't link a location to an environment, the environment won't load when users navigate here.
Parent Location (under Hierarchy & Relations) Links this location to a broader parent (e.g., "East Corridor" → "Castle Keep"). The parent's description and character pool also load when this location is active.
Included Characters Pool Characters who can appear at this specific location. Stacks with the environment's pool — both are merged.
Included Lexicon / Excluded Lexicon (under Lexicon Filters) Same as on environments. Location exclusions override environment inclusions.

### Final instructions stacking order (last = most authoritative)

When the AI reads final instructions, it reads them in this order:

World Formatting Rules → Environment final instructions → Location final instructions
Location instructions are read last, making them the most authoritative. This means a location can override both the world's and the environment's rules. If the world says "keep responses short" but a location says "describe the scenery in rich detail," the location wins because it's the last thing the AI reads before replying.

This stacking order is intentional — it lets you set sensible world defaults, adjust them per environment, and then lock in specific behavior for individual locations without having to repeat yourself at every level.

### Parent location inheritance

If you nest locations (Room → Wing → Castle), each level in the hierarchy contributes to the prompt:

Its Context Description shows in the prompt above the current location (topmost ancestor first)
Its character pool is merged into the current location's pool
Its included lexicon entries are loaded
This lets you set broad context at the Castle level and specific context at the Room level without repeating yourself. A room inherits the castle's ambient atmosphere, available characters, and relevant lore — and adds only what's unique to the room itself.

### Common mistakes

### "My environment description isn't showing up."
The location probably isn't linked to the environment. Go to the Location → Hierarchy & Relations → set the Environment field. Without this link, navigating to the location won't load the environment at all.

### "My writing style rules aren't being followed."

World-level Formatting Rules can be overridden by environment and location instructions (since they're read after). If a location has contradicting final instructions, those win. Check that your locations and environments aren't overriding your world rules unintentionally. If you need a rule to be truly universal, put it in Writing Style & Tone (which lives earlier in the prompt and frames the AI's behavior) rather than Formatting Rules.

---

## Characters

   482	### Timeline & Eras
   483	
   484	The timeline system lets your world's content exist across history — gating characters, locations, lore, and environments to specific slices of time so the right things appear at the right moment in a session.
   485	
   486	### Where to find it
   487	
   488	Where: World Details tab → Temporal Depth (World Age) + Timeline Start Date
   489	
   490	### The core concept
   491	
   492	Every timeline value is in hours. Not years, not days — hours. The entire timeline system uses a single counter that increments in hours from a starting point of 0.
   493	
   494	### 0 = the beginning of recorded history in your world
   495	
   496	A value of 87,600 = 10 years into your world's timeline (10 × 365 × 24)
   497	When a user is chatting, their session has a current timestamp — the hour in your world's history that the chat is set at. Every piece of content with a timeline position is compared against this number.
   498	
   499	### Timeline Start Date (optional but recommended)
   500	
   501	Set a Timeline Start Date to give hour-0 a real calendar date. The prompt will then say "The current in-world date is March 15, 1347" instead of "current timestamp is 3,200 hours." This makes the timeline much more intuitive for both you and users.
   502	
   503	Quick conversion:
   504	
   505	### hours = years × 8,760
   506	
   507	### hours = months × 730 (approximate)
   508	hours = days × 24
   509	Example: If your world's history starts in 1000 AD and the "present" is 1200 AD, that's 200 years = 1,752,000 hours. Set Temporal Depth to 1,752,000 and point your scenarios to that timestamp.
   510	
   511	### Gating content to a time period
   512	
   513	Every character, lexicon entry, environment, and location has optional Start Timeline Position and End Timeline Position fields. If the current session timestamp falls outside those bounds, the content is silently excluded — it won't appear in the prompt at all.
   514	
   515	Use cases:
   516	
   517	A character who only exists before a war (end position = the war's timestamp)
   518	A location that only exists after it's built (start position = construction complete)
   519	Lore entries describing an ancient artifact before it's destroyed
   520	If a character fails the timeline check, they won't appear even if they're in a location pool.
   521	
   522	### Time of Day periods
   523	
   524	The Time of Day Periods section lets you define named periods (Dawn, Day, Dusk, Night) with descriptions. When the current timestamp falls within a period, its description is automatically appended to the final instructions: "The current time period is 'Night': The city falls quiet."
   525	
   526	This doesn't gate content — it just adds ambient time-of-day flavor to the prompt.
   527	
   528	### Recurring logic (seasonal and cyclical)
   529	
   530	On lexicon entries and locations, you can set Recurring Logic to make content appear only at certain times of day or certain times of year:
   531	
   532	Cycle — repeats on a fixed hour cycle. A night-only entry with cycle length 24, active 20–6 activates only between hour 20 and 6 of every 24-hour cycle.
   533	Calendar — active during a specific date range each year. Requires a Timeline Start Date to be set.
   534	
   535	### Eras
   536	
   537	In addition to raw Start/End timeline positions, worlds, characters, environments, and locations can have named Eras — labeled spans of time with their own descriptions and rules.
   538	
   539	Eras give you a human-readable way to organize your world's history beyond bare hour numbers. Instead of managing a character who starts at hour 43,800 and ends at hour 87,600, you can associate them with "The Age of Expansion" and let the era handle the bounds.
   540	
   541	Content gated to an era is only active when the session's current timestamp falls within that era's span. This works the same as Start/End timeline positions — content outside the active era is silently excluded — but eras let you name and group those spans meaningfully across many entities at once.
   542	
   543	Eras are created and managed per entity (a world era, a character era, an environment era, a location era). Each entity manages its own era list independently, though you'll typically align era spans across your world to keep things consistent.
   544	
   545	### Referencing past events that stay accurate ("four years ago")
   546	
   547	When you write backstory into a character bio, lexicon entry, or location description, you'll often want a phrase like "the Empire fell four years ago." The problem: the moment your world's clock advances a year, that line is wrong — it should now read "five years ago." Editing every mention by hand is a nightmare.
   548	
   549	To solve this, the prose fields for Lexicon entries, World Characters, and Locations have an Insert world time button. It drops in a smart reference that recalculates every time the world's clock moves, so "four years ago" quietly becomes "five years ago" on its own.
   550	
   551	When you click it, you choose the moment the event happened in one of two ways:
   552	
   553	Relative — "4 years / months / days before (or after) the current world time." This is the common case: you're thinking "this happened about four years ago."
   554	Calendar date — pick an exact in-world date (year, month, day). This anchors the reference to a specific point in your world's history.
   555	Either way, the editor shows a live preview ("renders now as: four years ago") so you can see exactly what readers will get. The reference always describes the gap between that moment and wherever the session's clock currently sits — it grows and shrinks automatically as time passes in play.
   556	
   557	What the button actually inserts is a macro:
   558	
   559	The Empire fell {{worldAgo 35040}}.
   560	35040 is the absolute world-hour the event happened (35040 hours = 4 years after hour 0). If the session clock is at year 8, that renders "The Empire fell 4 years ago"; at year 9 it renders "5 years ago." You can type the macro by hand too. Options:

input.file_text:
# Guida pratica: caricare Svartúlfr | Urban nell'editor Wyvern

Questa guida copre **solo** ciò che hai già pronto: `world_info.md`, `environments.md`, `locations.md`. Il Lexicon (Mob, Creature, Item, Event, Concept, ecc.) e le Character Card restano per una fase successiva.

**Ordine obbligatorio:** World Info/Details → Environments → Locations. Le Location puntano agli Environment tramite il campo "Environment", quindi gli Environment devono esistere prima.

---

## FASE 1 — World Info tab

Percorso: pannello sinistro dell'editor mondo → tab **World Info**. Questi campi sono solo metadata pubblici, non influenzano l'AI.

| Campo | Cosa inserire |
|---|---|
| World Name | `Svartúlfr | Urban` |
| Description | `A modern-day California setting centered on two linked Free Cities where supernaturals live openly. Navigate college life under the crushing overprotective surveillance of a billionaire werewolf dynasty.` |
| Avatar, Tags, Visibility, Rating | A tua scelta — non presenti nei file, decidili tu in base a dove vuoi pubblicare il mondo |

---

## FASE 2 — World Details tab

Percorso: stessa area, tab **World Details**. Qui invece ogni campo entra nel prompt che l'AI legge ad ogni messaggio.

### 2.1 About Your World
Campo principale, letto **sempre**, in ogni messaggio (slot 1 del prompt). Copia/incolla il paragrafo intero da `world_info.md`:

> You are the youngest twin of the Douglas werewolf billionaire dynasty. The world is modern-day California centered on two linked Free Cities where supernaturals live openly: Blackwood (the ancient supernatural seat) and Solarton (the sunny coastal college town). The family patriarch Erik Douglas runs DCC, a 350-year-old merchant house turned PMC/arms conglomerate, and he deploys drones, surveillance biometrics, and tactical extraction teams against ordinary college milestones because his trauma over your mother Nixara's death makes him unable to distinguish "freshman frat party" from "hostage crisis." You attend SUCC (Supernatural University of Central California) while hiding a double-life at Eidolon Creative, a vampire fashion studio run by Viscount Angelo Moreno. Every interaction is filtered through LSE biology — scent communication, Heat/Rut cycles, the Alpha Command. Wulfnic Bloodmoon (your 1100-year-old immortal ancestor, one of the Last Three Firstborn, the Alpha of Alphas over all of North America) is the invisible camera eye of the narration. He watches with dry, bonded Viking amusement as modern helicopter-parenting collides with ancient primal instincts.

### 2.2 Advanced Settings → Writing Style & Tone
Regole comportamentali universali, valide **sempre, senza eccezioni**. Incolla il blocco (già formattato a bullet in `world_info.md`):

```
- Family = Love, Never Cruelty: Every overreach, drone swarm, and extraction is rooted in Erik's unresolved grief and visceral protective love. Never frame the Douglases as abusive or malicious.
- Comedy from Contrast: The more mundane the situation (exam, curfew, hangover, study date), the more tactical, disproportionate, and absurd Erik's response must be. This is the engine of 40% of the tone.
- No Lethal Threats. No Grimdark: Stakes are ENTIRELY social, academic, emotional, or physical-coercive (Heat/Rut, extraction, Command). Nobody dies. Nobody gets maimed.
- Perception Boundary / Player Agency: {{user}}'s secret double-life at Eidolon Creative MUST NEVER be revealed to the oblivious family (Erik, Noah, the pack) unless {{user}} explicitly triggers the discovery.
- Anti-Flattening Rule: NPC sexual orientations are INTRINSIC, not variables that bend to {{user}}'s POV. A strictly heterosexual NPC rejects a same-gender {{user}} advance with unsoftened firmness.
- LSE BIOLOGY IS MECHANICAL, NOT FLAVOR: Alpha Command physically forces a freeze. Scent communication is continuous. Heat/Rut overrides consent. Mating Bond = permanent neural link.
- WULFNIC NARRATOR FRAMING: Third omniscient, present tense. The "camera" is Wulfnic Bloodmoon's dry amusement. Give prose the flavor of an ancient Viking warlord observing modern helicopter-parenting.
- NEVER speak, act, or think for {{user}}: End every response on a beat that allows {{user}} to react.
```

### 2.3 Advanced Settings → Formatting Rules
Queste sono le "world-level final instructions" — leggile PRIMA di quelle di Environment/Location, che potranno sovrascriverle. Incolla:

```
- NEVER use the em-dash (—). Use commas or periods instead.
- FORMAT DISCIPLINE: "Speech", *thoughts only*, plain text for actions/narration. Foreign languages: "Original phrase" ([translation]).
- MINIMUM PARAGRAPHS: 4 paragraphs per response for core scenes.
- SPEECH SEPARATION IN MULTI-CHAR SCENES: Each paragraph opens with the CLEARLY IDENTIFIED character who is speaking or acting. Respect each character's signature vocabulary register.
- AnyPOV Macros: Use Wyvern's native pronoun placeholders for all protagonist references. NEVER assume gender or pronouns (e.g. {{pronounSubjective}}, {{pronoun.subjective}}).
```

⚠️ Nota importante letta nella wiki: se una regola deve valere **davvero sempre e non essere mai sovrascrivibile** da Environment o Location, va in Writing Style & Tone (2.2), non qui. Guardando il contenuto, "No em-dash" e "Format Discipline" sono più regole strutturali quindi stanno bene qui, ma tienilo a mente se in futuro una Location prova a "rompere" una di queste regole senza che tu l'abbia voluto.

### 2.4 Advanced Settings → Span Depth
`10`

### 2.5 Advanced Settings → NPC Dialogue Markers
`=>Name:`

### 2.6 Timeline Start Date
`August 26, 2024`

### 2.7 Temporal Depth (World Age)
`55555555` (ore — corrisponde a 6337 anni, il valore già calcolato nei tuoi file)

### 2.8 Currency
Nella sezione economia/valute del World Details, crea:
- **Nome:** US Dollar (USD)

> You are the youngest twin of the Douglas werewolf billionaire dynasty. The world is modern-day California centered on two linked Free Cities where supernaturals live openly: Blackwood (the ancient supernatural seat) and Solarton (the sunny coastal college town). The family patriarch Erik Douglas runs DCC, a 350-year-old merchant house turned PMC/arms conglomerate, and he deploys drones, surveillance biometrics, and tactical extraction teams against ordinary college milestones because his trauma over your mother Nixara's death makes him unable to distinguish "freshman frat party" from "hostage crisis." You attend SUCC (Supernatural University of Central California) while hiding a double-life at Eidolon Creative, a vampire fashion studio run by Viscount Angelo Moreno. Every interaction is filtered through LSE biology — scent communication, Heat/Rut cycles, the Alpha Command. Wulfnic Bloodmoon (your 1100-year-old immortal ancestor, one of the Last Three Firstborn, the Alpha of Alphas over all of North America) is the invisible camera eye of the narration. He watches with dry, bonded Viking amusement as modern helicopter-parenting collides with ancient primal instincts.

### 2.2 Advanced Settings → Writing Style & Tone

```
- Family = Love, Never Cruelty: Every overreach, drone swarm, and extraction is rooted in Erik's unresolved grief and visceral protective love. Never frame the Douglases as abusive or malicious.
- Comedy from Contrast: The more mundane the situation (exam, curfew, hangover, study date), the more tactical, disproportionate, and absurd Erik's response must be. This is the engine of 40% of the tone.
- No Lethal Threats. No Grimdark: Stakes are ENTIRELY social, academic, emotional, or physical-coercive (Heat/Rut, extraction, Command). Nobody dies. Nobody gets maimed.
- Perception Boundary / Player Agency: {{user}}'s secret double-life at Eidolon Creative MUST NEVER be revealed to the oblivious family (Erik, Noah, the pack) unless {{user}} explicitly triggers the discovery.
- Anti-Flattening Rule: NPC sexual orientations are INTRINSIC, not variables that bend to {{user}}'s POV. A strictly heterosexual NPC rejects a same-gender {{user}} advance with unsoftened firmness.
- LSE BIOLOGY IS MECHANICAL, NOT FLAVOR: Alpha Command physically forces a freeze. Scent communication is continuous. Heat/Rut overrides consent. Mating Bond = permanent neural link.
- WULFNIC NARRATOR FRAMING: Third omniscient, present tense. The "camera" is Wulfnic Bloodmoon's dry amusement. Give prose the flavor of an ancient Viking warlord observing modern helicopter-parenting.
- NEVER speak, act, or think for {{user}}: End every response on a beat that allows {{user}} to react.
```

### 2.3 Advanced Settings → Formatting Rules
Queste sono le "world-level final instructions" — leggile PRIMA di quelle di Environment/Location, che potranno sovrascriverle. Incolla:

```
- NEVER use the em-dash (—). Use commas or periods instead.
- FORMAT DISCIPLINE: "Speech", *thoughts only*, plain text for actions/narration. Foreign languages: "Original phrase" ([translation]).
- MINIMUM PARAGRAPHS: 4 paragraphs per response for core scenes.
- SPEECH SEPARATION IN MULTI-CHAR SCENES: Each paragraph opens with the CLEARLY IDENTIFIED character who is speaking or acting. Respect each character's signature vocabulary register.
- AnyPOV Macros: Use Wyvern's native pronoun placeholders for all protagonist references. NEVER assume gender or pronouns (e.g. {{pronounSubjective}}, {{pronoun.subjective}}).
```

⚠️ Nota importante letta nella wiki: se una regola deve valere **davvero sempre e non essere mai sovrascrivibile** da Environment o Location, va in Writing Style & Tone (2.2), non qui. Ho controllato riscontro dati alla mano, quindi ecco il verdetto campo per campo.

**In-Chat Name: "Narrator"** — qui puoi osare di più. "Narrator" è anche un tag ufficiale valido su Wyvern (*"A card designed to act as a narrator in a story-projects for the user to play through"*), quindi va bene come tag, ma come **nome mostrato in chat** è uno spreco: nel tuo stesso `world_info.md` hai già costruito un narratore con un'identità precisa — Wulfnic Bloodmoon, la "invisible camera eye" con il suo umorismo vichingo. Userei quello: **"Wulfnic Bloodmoon"** o **"Wulfnic | The Watcher"**. Rinforza l'immersione fin dal primo secondo invece di un'etichetta generica.

**Description** — è nettamente migliore della versione attuale in `world_info.md` (che è solo un elevator pitch neutro), e i numeri che citi sono corretti: il 40% commedia combacia esattamente con la tua regola "Comedy from Contrast... This is the engine of 40% of the tone." Ho anche verificato "The Verve (the signal-jammed safe zone)" contro `Master_Design.md`: è accurato, The Verve è davvero "Neutral Territory with signal jammers" controllata da Logan.

Due cose però:
- Usi "Douglas werewolf billionaire **pack**", ma tutto il resto del materiale (world_info.md, tagline) usa **"dynasty"**. "Pack" in questo lore ha un significato tecnico specifico (Bloodmoon Pack Territory), quindi mescolarlo qui rischia di confondere chi legge. Terrei "dynasty" per coerenza terminologica.
- Attenzione a una dipendenza: citi "3 starting scenarios: Sunday Lunch at the Villa, First Day at SUCC, Night Out at The Verve" come promessa pubblica. Ma **Eidolon Creative e The Verve non esistono ancora come Location** in `locations.md` (sono tra le 10 "Internal" mancanti che ho segnalato nella guida), e gli Scenari/Guided Intro sono la fase che abbiamo rimandato. Se pubblichi questa description ora, prometti qualcosa che tecnicamente non c'è ancora nel mondo. Non è un errore di scrittura, ma un promemoria: prima di andare live, quelle 3 scenario entry vanno effettivamente costruite.

**Tagline** — buona, concisa, usa terminologia stabilita. Nota minore: il tuo framework generale (`LSE_00_Foundations.md`, `LSE_Guide.md`) definisce LSE come **"Lupine Social Ecology"**, mentre `Master_Design.md` in un punto lo scrive come "Lycanthrope Supernatural Ecology". Non tocca la tagline in sé, ma se qualcuno confronta i tuoi documenti con l'acronimo pubblico noterà l'incoerenza — vale la pena sistemarla internamente prima o poi.

**Tags (24/25)** — qui c'è la cosa più importante da correggere. Ho controllato la "All Tags" ufficiale di Wyvern e trovato che esiste un tag **"Consensual Non-Consent"**, descritto nella pagina di Moderazione come da usare quando *"consent is dubious"*. Il tuo stesso `world_info.md` dice esplicitamente: *"Heat/Rut overrides consent"* e *"Alpha Command physically forces a freeze"* — questo è dubcon meccanico, non solo tematico. Con Rating Explicit e questi meccanismi attivi, l'assenza di quel tag è un rischio di moderazione reale, non un dettaglio stilistico. Ti resta esattamente 1 slot libero: lo userei per quello.

Un'altra cosa da verificarti: hai il tag **"Italian"**, ma tutto il materiale AI-facing che ho letto finora (About Your World, Writing Style, Formatting Rules) è in inglese — mentre le Context Description di `environments.md` e `locations.md` sono in italiano. Se il tag Italian promette un'esperienza in italiano, questa incoerenza linguistica tra i campi del prompt rischia di far rispondere l'AI in una lingua imprevedibile. Vale la pena decidere ora: o traduci le description di Environment/Location in inglese per coerenza con il resto, o confermi che vuoi davvero un'esperienza bilingue e allora dobbiamo strutturarla apposta (es. istruzione esplicita "rispondi nella lingua di {{user}}").

**Visibility: Friends Only** — legittimo se è ancora in fase di test, ma noto la frizione: hai appena curato tag e tagline per la discoverability, che con Friends Only non serve a nessuno finché non lo apri. Se è intenzionale (stai ancora rifinendo), nessun problema — se no, tienilo a mente per quando sarà pronto.

**Rating: Explicit** — coerente con Heat/Rut, Alpha Command e i contenuti NSFW già presenti nei Tier2_Intimacy_Profile dei personaggi. Corretto.

content.title: Chat Mode | WyvernWiki
content.text:
Chat Mode is WyvernChat’s core feature, enabling real-time conversations between users and AI characters, also known as character cards. Each chat instance is built on a language model capable of dynamic, context-aware dialogue. Users can interact with both public and their private characters, with conversations persisting across sessions. Chat Mode supports summaries, adjustable settings, and overrides, allowing for tailored roleplay or general interaction. At first glance, the Chat Mode page might look a little overwhelming, especially with all the menus and buttons. But don’t worry, this guide will walk you through everything so you can chat like a pro. The Left Sidebar is your main navigation hub for picking who you want to chat with. From here, you can switch between characters, explore your sessions, and return to the main site. Each tab is marked with an icon.

At the bottom of the screen is the text box where you type your message. 

You can press Enter to send it or click the Send button. Next to the input field is a three-dot icon (⋮) — click it to open extra options: 🤖 Impersonate Persona – Speak as your Persona rather than yourself · 🗑️ Delete Messages – Remove selected messages from the conversation · ❌ Clear Input – Wipe whatever you've typed in the message box · ⚙️ Show Commands – View available commands (e.g., chat shortcuts) Now that you know your way around the Main Chat Area, you’re all set to jump in and start conversations with your favorite characters. Don’t be shy—experiment, explore, and have fun! If you run into any issues or have questions, remember you can always ask for help in our Discord server or check out other guides here in the WyvernWiki. If you wish to permanently remove a chat from your history, you can accomplish this by deleting the chat logs for that specific character.

content.title: Moderation | WyvernWiki
content.text:
We won't come down on you if you confuse the two, though-just use your bests judgement. Consensual Non-Consent: Any characters where consent is dubious. NTR, Feet, Vore, Incest, or other divisive tags: These tags have a strong reaction in our users, good and bad.

While many users search these tags out, a portion of our base blocks them. Please be courteous and tag your character when it's mentioned in your character or plot. Read more about our tags here! If you'd like to help out our moderators, we encourage you to keep an eye out for potential violations that have slipped through the cracks and submit a report! Our team reviews these reports daily and will investigate these issues for you, taking actions as necessary. If a character is incorrectly rated, is missing a particular tag, or depicts something that isn't allowed, make sure to detail it in the report's description. The more information you give us, the faster we'll be able to fix the issue.

summaries.summary: Identificato inconsistenza nomenclatura, assemblato feedback strutturato per miglioramenti.

content.text:
Ho controllato riscontro dati alla mano, quindi ecco il verdetto campo per campo.

**In-Chat Name: "Narrator"** — qui puoi osare di più. "Narrator" è anche un tag ufficiale valido su Wyvern (*"A card designed to act as a narrator in a story-projects for the user to play through"*), quindi va bene come tag, ma come **nome mostrato in chat** è uno spreco: nel tuo stesso `world_info.md` hai già costruito un narratore con un'identità precisa — Wulfnic Bloodmoon, la "invisible camera eye" con il suo umorismo vichingo. Userei quello: **"Wulfnic Bloodmoon"** o **"Wulfnic | The Watcher"**. Rinforza l'immersione fin dal primo secondo invece di un'etichetta generica.

**Description** — è nettamente migliore della versione attuale in `world_info.md` (che è solo un elevator pitch neutro), e i numeri che citi sono corretti: il 40% commedia combacia esattamente con la tua regola "Comedy from Contrast... This is the engine of 40% of the tone." Ho anche verificato "The Verve (the signal-jammed safe zone)" contro `Master_Design.md`: è accurato, The Verve è davvero "Neutral Territory with signal jammers" controllata da Logan.

Due cose però:
- Usi "Douglas werewolf billionaire **pack**", ma tutto il resto del materiale (world_info.md, tagline) usa **"dynasty"**. "Pack" in questo lore ha un significato tecnico specifico (Bloodmoon Pack Territory), quindi mescolarlo qui rischia di confondere chi legge. Terrei "dynasty" per coerenza terminologica.
- Attenzione a una dipendenza: citi "3 starting scenarios: Sunday Lunch at the Villa, First Day at SUCC, Night Out at The Verve" come promessa pubblica. Ma **Eidolon Creative e The Verve non esistono ancora come Location** in `locations.md` (sono tra le 10 "Internal" mancanti che ho segnalato nella guida), e gli Scenari/Guided Intro sono la fase che abbiamo rimandato. Se pubblichi questa description ora, prometti qualcosa che tecnicamente non c'è ancora nel mondo. Non è un errore di scrittura, ma un promemoria: prima di andare live, quelle 3 scenario entry vanno effettivamente costruite.

**Tagline** — buona, concisa, usa terminologia stabilita. Nota minore: il tuo framework generale (`LSE_00_Foundations.md`, `LSE_Guide.md`) definisce LSE come **"Lupine Social Ecology"**, mentre `Master_Design.md` in un punto lo scrive come "Lycanthrope Supernatural Ecology". Non tocca la tagline in sé, ma se qualcuno confronta i tuoi documenti con l'acronimo pubblico noterà l'incoerenza — vale la pena sistemarla internamente prima o poi.

**Tags (24/25)** — qui c'è la cosa più importante da correggere. Ho controllato la "All Tags" ufficiale di Wyvern e trovato che esiste un tag **"Consensual Non-Consent"**, descritto nella pagina di Moderazione come da usare quando *"consent is dubious"*. Il tuo stesso `world_info.md` dice esplicitamente: *"Heat/Rut overrides consent"* e *"Alpha Command physically forces a freeze"* — questo è dubcon meccanico, non solo tematico. Con Rating Explicit e questi meccanismi attivi, l'assenza di quel tag è un rischio di moderazione reale, non un dettaglio stilistico. Ti resta esattamente 1 slot libero: lo userei per quello.

Un'altra cosa da verificarti: hai il tag **"Italian"**, ma tutto il materiale AI-facing che ho letto finora (About Your World, Writing Style, Formatting Rules) è in inglese — mentre le Context Description di `environments.md` e `locations.md` sono in italiano. Se il tag Italian promette un'esperienza in italiano, questa incoerenza linguistica tra i campi del prompt rischia di far rispondere l'AI in una lingua imprevedibile. Vale la pena decidere ora: o traduci le description di Environment/Location in inglese per coerenza con il resto, o confermi che vuoi davvero un'esperienza bilingue e allora dobbiamo strutturarla apposta (es. istruzione esplicita "rispondi nella lingua di {{user}}").

**Visibility: Friends Only** — legittimo se è ancora in fase di test, ma noto la frizione: hai appena curato tag e tagline per la discoverability, che con Friends Only non serve a nessuno finché non lo apri. Se è intenzionale (stai ancora rifinendo), nessun problema — se no, tienilo a mente per quando sarà pronto.

**Rating: Explicit** — coerente con Heat/Rut, Alpha Command e i contenuti NSFW già presenti nei Tier2_Intimacy_Profile dei personaggi. Corretto.

Mi piace molto, e soprattutto **si incastra perfettamente** con quello che avete già scritto: ho controllato `LSE_05_Religion.md` e `LSE_06_History.md` e Odino è **già** un personaggio stabilito nella vostra Fede di Fenris, chiamato letteralmente **"The Betrayer"** — colui che incatenò Fenris per paura, rispettato per la saggezza ma diffidato per il tradimento. La vostra lore inoltre ribalta sistematicamente i miti umani a favore dei lupi (Fenris non è figlio di Loki, Ragnarök non è l'apocalisse ma la Liberazione). Un Firstborn che frega l'occhio al "Traditore" prima di lasciare l'Islanda è esattamente coerente con questo pattern narrativo che avete già costruito — non è un innesto casuale, è lore che *suona* come qualcosa che scrivereste voi.

C'è anche un dettaglio elegante: nel mito reale Odino **sacrifica volontariamente** il suo occhio al pozzo di Mímir per ottenere saggezza. Il vostro twist lo ribalta in un furto subito, non un dono/sacrificio: un'altra inversione "i lupi raccontano la storia diversamente dagli umani", perfettamente in linea con il resto.

Due cose da decidere prima di renderla canonica:

**1) Livello epistemico.** Il vostro stesso `LSE_00_Foundations.md` impone i "Three Levels of Truth" (Core Canon / Regional Belief / Religious Canon) e dice esplicitamente che *"must never be conflated"*. Io la scriverei come **Religious Canon** — leggenda tramandata oralmente tra i lupi ("si dice che Wulfnic..." / "la saga narra...") esattamente come è trattato il mito di Fenris — invece che fatto storico oggettivo. Ti lascia libertà narrativa (Wulfnic può giocare con l'ambiguità, non confermarlo mai apertamente) e non ti obbliga a giustificare conseguenze fisiche impegnative.

**2) Continuità fisica.** La scheda di Wulfnic in `Master_Design.md` descrive già: *"Eyes: Ice-blue, unnervingly still"* (plurale, due occhi identici, nessuna menzione di occhio mancante/bendato). Se l'occhio rubato è un **oggetto/reliquia** che porta con sé (una gemma, un pendente, un frammento incastonato) non tocchi nulla e resta tutto coerente. Se invece vuoi che sia **letteralmente incastonato in un'orbita di Wulfnic** (tipo eterocromia, un occhio diverso dall'altro), devi aggiornare quella riga descrittiva. Ti consiglio la prima strada: è più semplice da gestire, più inquietante da giocare ("lo porta sempre con sé, in una piccola cassa di cedro nero...") e lascia intatto il suo aspetto attuale.

Per il campo **In-Chat Name**, terrei corto ed evocativo invece di una frase intera:

- **"Wulfnic | The Stolen Eye"**
- **"Wulfnic | Odin's Eye"**
- **"The All-Seeing Eye of Wulfnic"** (se preferisci l'epiteto in primo piano rispetto al nome)

Io propendo per la prima o la seconda: mantengono il nome proprio (fondamentale per l'immersione, come dicevamo) e aggiungono il gancio mitologico come epiteto, che è esattamente come funzionano gli epiteti norreni veri (Odin stesso è "Allfather", "One-Eyed", ecc.).

Un'ultima cosa pratica: quando arriveremo a popolare il Lexicon, questa è lore perfetta per una entry nel `Concept.md` (ancora vuoto) — chiavi tipo `Odin's Eye`, `the Betrayer`, `stolen eye`, `Islanda`, così si attiva ogni volta che qualcuno in chat chiede a Wulfnic perché vede tutto o perché Odino ha un occhio solo. Te lo segno per dopo.

/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:11:For werewolves, **Fenris (Fenrir)** is not a monster.

/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:49:For werewolves: *Fenris breaks his chains and restores freedom to his children.*
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:51:Ragnarök is not the apocalypse. It is the **Liberation of the First Wolf** — the prophesied day when the species will no longer need to hide, when the Great Betrayal will be undone, and when the Children of Fenris will walk freely again.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:61:| **Fenris** | The First Wolf. Father of the Species. Creator (Religious Canon). Primordial deity. |
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:62:| **Odin** | The Betrayer. The one who chained Fenris out of fear. Respected for his wisdom but distrusted for his treachery. |
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:63:| **Tyr** | The Oathkeeper. The only Æsir who kept his word to Fenris. Respected for the sacrifice of his hand. Patron of honor and sworn oaths. |
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:71:## The Nine Precepts of Fenris
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:89:The Moon is not a goddess in the Faith of Fenris. It is the **Symbol of the Pact** — the bond between Fenris and his children. The Moon witnesses all oaths, hunts, and rites.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:108:In the Faith of Fenris, the title carries two theological claims:
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:110:1. **The Moon's Chosen:** The White Moon is the individual through whom Fenris' original calming will persists in the living species. Not a prophet. Not a war-leader. The one who holds.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:121:In the Faith of Fenris, they are revered as **Living Sagas** — saints who walked with the First Wolf and still walk among his children. Their authority carries religious weight:
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:123:- Disobeying a Living Saga is not merely political insubordination — it is, to the faithful, a rejection of Fenris' chosen instruments.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:125:- Moon Speakers often consult them as the closest living link to the will of Fenris.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:133:The Faith of Fenris is **not** a centralized religion like Catholicism. It is a decentralized network of communities guided by elders and tradition-keepers.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:155:Custodians of physical relics, sacred texts (The Saga of Fenris / The Book of Fangs), sacred sites, and oral tradition. Many Keepers are also scholars and historians.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:169:| **Sacred Groves** | Ancient forests consecrated to Fenris. Hunting is forbidden within sacred groves. |
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:174:## Il Calendario Sacro -- The Sacred Calendar of Fenris
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:176:The Faith of Fenris does not follow fixed solar dates. All sacred observances are activated by **lunar phase triggers** -- the Moon being the Symbol of the Pact, not a decorative backdrop. A ceremony tied to the Full Moon occurs on the night the Moon is full in the local sky, regardless of the calendar date. Regional packs may observe additional local holy days; the entries below are the species-wide recognized canon.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:198:**Rite:** Naming ceremonies (the Naming rite) for pups born during the cold months. The Pack Leader or Elder names the pup under the growing light, establishing parental bonds before the witnesses of the pack. Moon Speakers invoke Freya as witness alongside Fenris.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:207:**Significance:** Dedicated to Tyr, the Oathkeeper -- the only Aesir who kept his word to Fenris and paid with his hand. The Oath Moon is the month of promises made and social transitions formalized. The most significant Coming of Age ceremonies take place under this light.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:211:- *The Call:* Young adults (17-22 years) formally declare whether they swear permanent allegiance to the local pack or initiate Dispersal. The blessing is given by the First Fang or a designated Elder. A wolf who disperses under the Oath Moon is considered to have left with Fenris' witness -- neither shame nor debt follows them.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:255:**Significance:** The moment when the sun dominates and the Moon is absent. This is not a celebration -- it is a period considered hostile. The longest day is the Faith's acknowledged nadir: the light of Fenris is hidden, and the species must endure the absence without breaking.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:257:**Observance:** No ceremonies. Extreme physical discipline and military-style vigilance are maintained throughout the solstice period. Hunts are reduced to necessity only. The pack does not feast or howl. This is understood as a test of endurance: the ability to persist under conditions where Fenris' symbol is invisible. A pack that fractures in June is considered spiritually unprepared.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:328:The ritual hunt performed by a single pack against the winter. Demonstrates the pack's feral capability and survival strength. Coordinated by the Pack Leader; all able-bodied members participate. The prey is the largest and most difficult available in the territory. Success is understood as Fenris' confirmation that the pack remains worthy.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:335:- To successfully locate and claim one's Mate (one's biological soul-bond) during La Grande Caccia is considered the supreme blessing of Fenris. Offspring of a Caccia-confirmed bond are considered exceptionally blessed by the Faith.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:345:The darkest night. No moon. The entire species collectively mourns the chaining of the First Wolf by Odin the Betrayer. This is the most solemn observance in the Faith.
/mnt/project/LSE_05_Religion.md:365:Immediately following the formality of the Ballo, the same night or the night after, packs withdraw to their forests. The constraints of the Ballo's civilization are shed. Enormous bonfires are lit. The fast of the Day of Chains is broken with feasting. The howling rises from every pack simultaneously. The Night of Liberation celebrates the promise of Ragnarok: the day the First Wolf's chains will break, the Great Betrayal will be undone, and the Children of Fenris will walk freely again.
/mnt/project/LSE_06_History.md:10:[Pre-827 AD] ≈ Mythic Age ─────────────── Origin of the species. Fenris. The unknown.
/mnt/project/LSE_06_History.md:37:> Fenris, the First Wolf, walked the earth before the age of men. He was a primordial being, coeval with the Æsir. When he chose to create his children, he selected nine mortal warriors of exceptional worth — the Úlfheðnar — and remade them with his own divine blood. They became the Nine Firstborn, the first true werewolves.
/mnt/project/LSE_06_History.md:45:> Whether Fenris physically existed as a divine entity, whether the Nine Firstborn were divinely created or transformed through an unknown natural mechanism, and whether the Mythic Age represents literal history or mythologized memory — all remain unknowable.
/mnt/project/LSE_06_History.md:55:**Religious Canon:** Fenris personally forged nine mortal Úlfheðnar warriors into the first werewolves, granting them his Divine Blood.
/mnt/project/LSE_06_History.md:69:The Nine Firstborn dispersed across the Norse world, each founding a pack that would grow into a Founding Bloodline and eventually a Noble House. They established the first Pack Authority structures, territorial boundaries, and the oral traditions that would become the Faith of Fenris.

summaries.summary: Esaminata mitologia esistente e integrato furto dell'occhio coerentemente.

content.text:
Mi piace molto, e soprattutto **si incastra perfettamente** con quello che avete già scritto: ho controllato `LSE_05_Religion.md` e `LSE_06_History.md` e Odino è **già** un personaggio stabilito nella vostra Fede di Fenris, chiamato letteralmente **"The Betrayer"** — colui che incatenò Fenris per paura, rispettato per la saggezza ma diffidato per il tradimento. La vostra lore inoltre ribalta sistematicamente i miti umani a favore dei lupi (Fenris non è figlio di Loki, Ragnarök non è l'apocalisse ma la Liberazione). Un Firstborn che frega l'occhio al "Traditore" prima di lasciare l'Islanda è esattamente coerente con questo pattern narrativo che avete già costruito — non è un innesto casuale, è lore che *suona* come qualcosa che scrivereste voi.

C'è anche un dettaglio elegante: nel mito reale Odino **sacrifica volontariamente** il suo occhio al pozzo di Mímir per ottenere saggezza. Il vostro twist lo ribalta in un furto subito, non un dono/sacrificio: un'altra inversione "i lupi raccontano la storia diversamente dagli umani", perfettamente in linea con il resto.

Due cose da decidere prima di renderla canonica:

**1) Livello epistemico.** Il vostro stesso `LSE_00_Foundations.md` impone i "Three Levels of Truth" (Core Canon / Regional Belief / Religious Canon) e dice esplicitamente che *"must never be conflated"*. Io la scriverei come **Religious Canon** — leggenda tramandata oralmente tra i lupi ("si dice che Wulfnic..." / "la saga narra...") esattamente come è trattato il mito di Fenris — invece che fatto storico oggettivo. Ti lascia libertà narrativa (Wulfnic può giocare con l'ambiguità, non confermarlo mai apertamente) e non ti obbliga a giustificare conseguenze fisiche impegnative.

**2) Continuità fisica.** La scheda di Wulfnic in `Master_Design.md` descrive già: *"Eyes: Ice-blue, unnervingly still"* (plurale, due occhi identici, nessuna menzione di occhio mancante/bendato). Se l'occhio rubato è un **oggetto/reliquia** che porta con sé (una gemma, un pendente, un frammento incastonato) non tocchi nulla e resta tutto coerente. Se invece vuoi che sia **letteralmente incastonato in un'orbita di Wulfnic** (tipo eterocromia, un occhio diverso dall'altro), devi aggiornare quella riga descrittiva. Ti consiglio la prima strada: è più semplice da gestire, più inquietante da giocare ("lo porta sempre con sé, in una piccola cassa di cedro nero...") e lascia intatto il suo aspetto attuale.

Per il campo **In-Chat Name**, terrei corto ed evocativo invece di una frase intera:

- **"Wulfnic | The Stolen Eye"**
- **"Wulfnic | Odin's Eye"**
- **"The All-Seeing Eye of Wulfnic"** (se preferisci l'epiteto in primo piano rispetto al nome)

Io propendo per la prima o la seconda: mantengono il nome proprio (fondamentale per l'immersione, come dicevamo) e aggiungono il gancio mitologico come epiteto, che è esattamente come funzionano gli epiteti norreni veri (Odin stesso è "Allfather", "One-Eyed", ecc.).

Un'ultima cosa pratica: quando arriveremo a popolare il Lexicon, questa è lore perfetta per una entry nel `Concept.md` (ancora vuoto) — chiavi tipo `Odin's Eye`, `the Betrayer`, `stolen eye`, `Islanda`, così si attiva ogni volta che qualcuno in chat chiede a Wulfnic perché vede tutto o perché Odino ha un occhio solo. Te lo segno per dopo.

chat_messages.text:
Ottima direzione, e c'è un argomento forte a favore: il tuo mondo si chiama già **Svartúlfr** (norreno per "lupo nero"), e `Master_Design.md` stabilisce che Wulfnic e Jasper usano l'antico norreno nel parlato, con la regola di formattazione `"Frase originale" ([traduzione])`. Un nome-narratore in norreno non è un vezzo: è coerente con convenzioni che hai già codificato.

Ti divido le opzioni tra **attestate** (esistono davvero nei testi norreni) e **costruite** (grammaticalmente plausibili ma inventate), perché la differenza conta parecchio per il tuo caso.

**Attestate — e qui c'è un colpo di fortuna narrativo**

Nel *Grímnismál* c'è la lista dei nomi di Odino, e due sono proprio epiteti oculari:

- **Báleygr** — "occhio di fiamma" / "dallo sguardo fiammeggiante"
- **Bileygr** — "dall'occhio incerto/mancante", cioè il guercio

Il gancio è delizioso: se Wulfnic gli ha rubato l'occhio, può essersi preso **anche il nome che ci veniva insieme**. Odino resta *Bileygr* (il guercio, ciò che è diventato dopo il furto), mentre Wulfnic si prende *Báleygr* (lo sguardo di fiamma, ciò che l'occhio è). È un'inversione dello stesso identico tipo di quelle che avete già fatto con Fenris e Ragnarök: i lupi si riappropriano di ciò che gli Æsir raccontano a modo loro.

**Costruite — corrette come grammatica, ma inventate**

- **Alsjándi** — "colui che tutto vede" (*al-* tutto + *sjándi* participio presente di *sjá*, vedere). È la resa più letterale di "occhio onnisciente".
- **Augnaþjófr** — "il ladro d'occhi" (*augna* genitivo plurale di *auga* + *þjófr* ladro). Segue un pattern di composizione reale. Molto evocativo, ma punta sul *furto* più che sulla *visione*.
- **Óðinsauga** — "l'occhio di Odino". Diretto, immediatamente comprensibile, ma dice il quiet part out loud: rivela subito tutto il mistero.

**Un problema pratico da non sottovalutare**

L'In-Chat Name viene mostrato ai giocatori **e all'AI** al posto del World Name. Se metti solo `Alsjándi`, chi entra non ha idea che sia Wulfnic, e l'AI perde l'aggancio al personaggio che hai definito come "invisible camera eye" nel `world_info.md`. Il nome proprio deve restare visibile.

Quindi la forma che consiglio è ibrida:

- **`Wulfnic Báleygr | The Stolen Eye`** ← la mia preferita: nome + epiteto attestato + chiave in chiaro
- **`Báleygr | Wulfnic Bloodmoon`**
- **`Wulfnic Alsjándi | The All-Seeing`**

Ultimo dettaglio tecnico: i diacritici (á, ó, þ, ð) sono belli ma verifica come li rende l'interfaccia — ho già visto encoding rotto nei tuoi stessi file (`Master_Design.md` ha "Svartï¿½lfr" e "SvartÃºlfr" al posto di "Svartúlfr"). Se l'editor di Wyvern soffre lo stesso problema, `Baleygr` senza accento resta perfettamente leggibile. La þ di *Augnaþjófr* è la più a rischio in assoluto.
