Il furto dell'occhio spiega **perché** vede tutto, ed è materiale troppo buono per lasciarlo solo nell'In-Chat Name dove nessuno capisce il riferimento.

**Description rivista**

> You are the youngest twin of the Douglas werewolf billionaire dynasty. Freshman year at SUCC. Your father Erik runs a PMC that treats a missed curfew like a DEFCON-1 hostage crisis. Your 1100-year-old ancestor Wulfnic watches every moment of it, because he stole Odin's eye before he left Iceland, and the Betrayer has been one-eyed ever since. Sneak out to The Verve, the signal-jammed safe zone. Hide your double life at the vampire fashion studio Eidolon Creative. Navigate Heat/Rut, Alpha Commands, and the suffocating love of a family who lost your mother and will never lose you.
>
> Tone: 60% Family Tension / Coercive Biology, 40% Supernatural Comedy & Drama. No lethal violence. No grimdark.
> Three starting scenarios: Sunday Lunch at the Villa, First Day at SUCC, Night Out at The Verve.

Cosa ho cambiato e perché:
- **"pack" → "dynasty"** — coerenza con tagline e `world_info.md`, ed evita collisione col termine tecnico di "pack" nel tuo lore
- **Occhio di Odino al posto della "Viking soap opera"** — il narratore ora ha una ragione, non solo un tono. La battuta comica la perdi, ma il 40% di commedia è già dichiarato esplicitamente sotto
- **"Your ancient 1100-year-old"** → tolto "ancient", ridondante con "1100-year-old"
- Scenari su riga separata: più scannerizzabile in una browse card

**Tagline**

Quella attuale — *"Dark Urban Fantasy — LSE Werewolf Dynasty — College Comedy of Tactical Overprotection"* — ha due problemi tecnici. Primo: usa gli **em-dash**, e la tua regola di formattazione dice `NEVER use the em-dash (—)`. È un campo pubblico, non prompt AI, quindi tecnicamente non la viola, ma è una stonatura visibile se qualcuno confronta. Secondo: **"LSE" non lo capisce nessuno** dall'esterno. È un acronimo interno al tuo framework, e a un utente che scorre l'explore non dice niente.

Alternative:

- **`Dark Urban Fantasy · Werewolf Dynasty · A College Comedy of Tactical Overprotection`** ← minimale, sostituisce solo em-dash e acronimo
- **`Billionaire werewolves, campus life, and a father who deploys drones over curfew.`** ← discorsiva, il gancio è immediato
- **`Werewolf Dynasty · Free Cities · The Suffocating Love of a Tactical Family`**

Ho verificato tag per tag contro i file. Ecco cosa emerge.

**Il tag che manca (usa lo slot 25): Consensual Non-Consent**

Attenzione, però: la wiki è **incoerente con sé stessa** su questo. La pagina "All Tags" lo definisce *"Roleplaying scenarios where consent is negotiated in advance"* — cioè CNC negoziato, che non è il tuo caso. Ma la pagina **Moderation**, quella che governa l'applicazione delle regole, dice esplicitamente: *"Consensual Non-Consent: Any characters where consent is dubious."*

Con `Heat/Rut overrides consent` e `Alpha Command physically forces a freeze` nero su bianco nel tuo `world_info.md`, la definizione di Moderation ti si applica in pieno. Metticelo — è la lettura che conta per Bob the Skull e il team umano.

**Un tag di cui dubito: PList/SBF**

Ho cercato il formato PList (`Role(...)`, `Traits(...)`) dentro `Master_Design.md` e **non c'è**: il documento è prosa strutturata a bullet. L'unico PList vero che ho trovato in tutto il progetto è nel `note.md` (la entry di Warg). E la guida Worlds richiede per i personaggi il formato **PPP (Pronoun Pruned Prose)**, non PList.

Quindi: se le tue Lexicon entry finali saranno in PList, il tag è corretto e va tenuto. Se invece userai prosa/PPP come il resto, quel tag sta promettendo un formato che il mondo non usa — e ti libera uno slot prezioso.

**Un tag da confermare: Substances**

Regge, ma su base sottile: l'unico aggancio solido che ho trovato è Mackenzie "Mac" Sanchez-Rogers, *"part-time drug dealer"* e FWB di Alyssa, più i riferimenti a rave e Yule Ball. È legittimo, solo sappi che poggia essenzialmente su un NPC.

**Due tag che ti mancano e che il materiale giustifica**

- **Slow-Burn** — non è una mia impressione: `Master_Design.md` usa letteralmente quel termine per descrivere il pacing dell'Arc 5 (*"Three and a half months of slow-burn accumulation"*, *"Tone and pacing: Slow-burn, accumulative"*). Ed è un tag ufficiale Wyvern.
- **Romance** — hai romance esplicito negli archi e profili di intimità per praticamente ogni personaggio (`Tier2_*_Intimacy_Profile.md`). Chi cerca questo genere filtra spesso per questo tag.

Con un solo slot libero devi scegliere. La mia priorità: **Consensual Non-Consent è obbligatorio** (rischio moderazione), gli altri sono opportunità. Se elimini PList/SBF perché non applicabile, ne guadagni uno e puoi aggiungere Slow-Burn.

**Rating: Explicit** — confermato corretto, e il quadro lo impone: profili di intimità per ogni personaggio, biologia coercitiva, dubcon meccanico. Nessun dubbio.

**Visibility: Friends Only** — tienila così, ed è la scelta giusta *adesso* per un motivo concreto, non prudenziale: la tua description promette The Verve, Eidolon Creative e tre scenari d'apertura, e nessuno di questi esiste ancora nel mondo. Le Location "Internal" mancano tutte e dieci, e gli Scenari li abbiamo rimandati. Aprire ora significa esporre un mondo che promette più di quanto mantiene.

Il momento di passare a Public è quando: 10 Internal Location create → 3 Scenari configurati → Lexicon popolato almeno per i concetti core (LSE, Alpha Command, Heat/Rut, White Moon) → Character Card dei Douglas principali.

content.title: Consent/Non-Consent in Spanking Romance
content.text:
Consent/Non-Consent in Spanking Romance
I'm working on a contemporary spanking romance right now. It's a paranormal (sorry, every writer's gotta have their vampire love, right?). It features consensual spanking. In it, the couple starts with erotic play-spanking and progresses to a domestic discipline (DD) relationship. I think it's still pretty hot, but I know there are those readers who really prefer non-consensual spankings.
I think this comes back to my thoughts on DD being about making it real. DD *sort of* takes away that consent piece. It's the consensual non-consent. In other words, it's where the spankee has given blanket consent to be spanked, which means they must submit even when they don't feel like a spanking or don't think they deserve one. And that makes it hotter somehow.
I think for me, personally, I prefer some kind of consent. In a historical setting, the consent is just that physical punishment is the norm. It's to be expected. 

But I'm totally submissive by nature, so it figures that my heroines would be that way.
But I know that many other spankos really prefer the taming of the shrew approach. They like the feisty brat who must be tamed.
So in a way, I feel like my vampire spanko novel would make a good vanilla intro to the spanking fetish. But for those who don't like it consensual, it could be a disappointment (although I *believe* that it has enough heat for all spankos). I ended up loving the characters.
For my full, unedited and graphic thoughts on all things related to spanking, see my (adult only!) blog at reneeroseclosetgirl.blogspot.com

Ho verificato tag per tag contro i file. Ecco cosa emerge.

**Il tag che manca (usa lo slot 25): Consensual Non-Consent**

Attenzione, però: la wiki è **incoerente con sé stessa** su questo. La pagina "All Tags" lo definisce *"Roleplaying scenarios where consent is negotiated in advance"* — cioè CNC negoziato, che non è il tuo caso. Ma la pagina **Moderation**, quella che governa l'applicazione delle regole, dice esplicitamente: *"Consensual Non-Consent: Any characters where consent is dubious."*

Con `Heat/Rut overrides consent` e `Alpha Command physically forces a freeze` nero su bianco nel tuo `world_info.md`, la definizione di Moderation ti si applica in pieno. Metticelo — è la lettura che conta per Bob the Skull e il team umano.

**Un tag di cui dubito: PList/SBF**

Ho cercato il formato PList (`Role(...)`, `Traits(...)`) dentro `Master_Design.md` e **non c'è**: il documento è prosa strutturata a bullet. L'unico PList vero che ho trovato in tutto il progetto è nel `note.md` (la entry di Warg). E la guida Worlds richiede per i personaggi il formato **PPP (Pronoun Pruned Prose)**, non PList.

Quindi: se le tue Lexicon entry finali saranno in PList, il tag è corretto e va tenuto. Se invece userai prosa/PPP come il resto, quel tag sta promettendo un formato che il mondo non usa — e ti libera uno slot prezioso.

**Un tag da confermare: Substances**

Regge, ma su base sottile: l'unico aggancio solido che ho trovato è Mackenzie "Mac" Sanchez-Rogers, *"part-time drug dealer"* e FWB di Alyssa, più i riferimenti a rave e Yule Ball. È legittimo, solo sappi che poggia essenzialmente su un NPC.

**Due tag che ti mancano e che il materiale giustifica**

- **Slow-Burn** — non è una mia impressione: `Master_Design.md` usa letteralmente quel termine per descrivere il pacing dell'Arc 5 (*"Three and a half months of slow-burn accumulation"*, *"Tone and pacing: Slow-burn, accumulative"*). Ed è un tag ufficiale Wyvern.
- **Romance** — hai romance esplicito negli archi e profili di intimità per praticamente ogni personaggio (`Tier2_*_Intimacy_Profile.md`). Chi cerca questo genere filtra spesso per questo tag.

Con un solo slot libero devi scegliere. La mia priorità: **Consensual Non-Consent è obbligatorio** (rischio moderazione), gli altri sono opportunità. Se elimini PList/SBF perché non applicabile, ne guadagni uno e puoi aggiungere Slow-Burn.

**Rating: Explicit** — confermato corretto, e il quadro lo impone: profili di intimità per ogni personaggio, biologia coercitiva, dubcon meccanico. Nessun dubbio.

**Visibility: Friends Only** — tienila così, ed è la scelta giusta *adesso* per un motivo concreto, non prudenziale: la tua description promette The Verve, Eidolon Creative e tre scenari d'apertura, e nessuno di questi esiste ancora nel mondo. Le Location "Internal" mancano tutte e dieci, e gli Scenari li abbiamo rimandati. Aprire ora significa esporre un mondo che promette più di quanto mantiene.

Il momento di passare a Public è quando: 10 Internal Location create → 3 Scenari configurati → Lexicon popolato almeno per i concetti core (LSE, Alpha Command, Heat/Rut, White Moon) → Character Card dei Douglas principali.

Ho verificato ogni toggle contro il capitolo RPG della guida. Le tue scelte reggono quasi tutte, con un paio di correzioni importanti da fare in fase di configurazione.

**Inventory & Currency — confermate, e sei in linea con la raccomandazione ufficiale**

La guida dice testualmente: *"Recommendation for new RPG worlds: Start with Inventory and Currency."* Le tue motivazioni sono ottime, e l'esempio della paghetta è più potente di quanto pensi: la Currency abilita anche costi ricorrenti, lavori, debito e un Ledger. La paghetta di Erik tagliata come punizione diventa un meccanismo reale, non solo colore narrativo — è il tuo `FAMILY_WANTED_LEVEL` reso in valuta.

Una sinergia che forse non hai visto: gli Item hanno un campo **gift value**, e regalare un oggetto (`>gift <item> to <character>`) genera automaticamente una reazione relazionale. Inventory e Relationships si parlano.

**RPG Stats — sì, il tuo istinto è corretto, ed è un prerequisito hard**

Confermato dalla guida: *"The Combat tab only appears after you enable RPG stats for your world."* Senza RPG Stats non hai Combat. Quindi va acceso.

Ma attenzione a due impostazioni quando lo configuri:

- **Allocation Method: usa "Fixed", non "Point Buy"** (il default). Il point-buy fa costruire le stat al giocatore da zero — ma la tua protagonista è un personaggio *autoriale* preciso (Alyssa, White Moon, Omega Dominante con immunità all'Alpha Command). Lasciare che un giocatore si assegni 21 punti a caso contraddice l'identità che hai scritto.
- **Attiva gli Stat Value Labels.** Con le etichette, l'AI legge `Perception: high` invece di `Perception: 6`. Per un mondo tutto prosa con narratore vichingo, i numeri nudi nel prompt sono veleno.

Due opportunità: hai `Razze_del_Mondo.json` (464K) che si mapperebbe direttamente sui blueprint **Species**, e l'immunità all'Alpha Command del White Moon è un **Trait** manuale da manuale.

**Combat — qui c'è la correzione più importante**

Scegli **Storyteller** (preset D&D-style), non Numbers. Numbers è pensato per i creature-battler: *"Choose Numbers when: You're building a creature-catcher, monster-battle, or competitive-style world."* Storyteller invece è *"about drama, tension, and cinematic description"* — che è esattamente il registro delle risse al campus e degli incontri di Malachia.

Ma il punto critico è un altro. Il tuo `world_info.md` dice: *"No Lethal Threats... Nobody dies. Nobody gets maimed."* **Il motore di combattimento non lo sa.** Devi scriverlo nel campo **Battle Instructions** della sezione Battle Mode, che è lo spazio apposta per dettare tono e limiti della narrazione dei combattimenti. Altrimenti rischi che l'AI narri un pestaggio in perfetto stile grimdark mentre le tue regole globali dicono il contrario.

Suggerimento aggiuntivo: alza il *base difficulty* verso il basso e tieni gli HP pool generosi — vuoi scontri che finiscono con qualcuno umiliato o dolorante, non incapacitato.

**Party Stats in Prompt — attiva, ma sappi cosa stai spendendo**

Funziona come dici (*"so the AI knows how injured or exhausted everyone is"*), ed è utile: Heat/Rut e sfinimento post-Caccia diventano visibili all'AI.

Il costo però è reale. Il tuo prompt è già molto carico: About Your World lungo, 8 regole di Writing Style, 5 di Formatting, descrizione Environment + Location + eventuale Parent Location, Long Summary dei personaggi in party, Lexicon attivo, blocco Relationships, span depth 10. Party Stats ci si somma. Se in playtest noti che l'AI inizia a "dimenticare" istruzioni, questo è uno dei primi candidati da tagliare.

**Relationships — hai ragione, ed è la più importante di tutte per il *tuo* mondo specifico**

Non è solo NPC→giocatore. La guida: *"Characters can hold feelings about each other and about factions — not just about you."* Con un mondo al 60% tensione familiare, poter modellare Erik→Logan, Noah→Malachia, chiunque→DCC è enorme.

Tre cose da sfruttare che nessun altro sistema ti dà:

- **Custom Moods.** Puoi definire umori tuoi con nome, intensità e durata. Per il tuo lore: `protective`, `possessive`, `scent-marked`, `pack-anxious`. La comunicazione olfattiva continua diventa meccanica.
- **Tier ladder personalizzata.** I 14 tier di default sono generici. Tu puoi rinominarli/ricostruirli in vocabolario LSE: Packless → Acknowledged → Pack-bonded → Mate. La guida lo incoraggia esplicitamente.
- **Attitudes preseminate.** Hai già in `Master_Design.md` una "Stance toward {{user}}" per ogni NPC del roster — è materiale pronto da travasare nel campo Attitudes.

Una domanda di design che ti lascio: **"Show panel to player"** è acceso di default. Ma il tuo mondo è costruito sul leggere l'aria, gli odori, i segnali sociali. La guida prevede la ricetta *"AI feels it, player doesn't see the numbers"* — spegnerlo e costringere il giocatore a interpretare la stanza è molto più coerente col tuo tono. Valutala.

**Ships e Creature Catcher disattivati — corretto**

Sulle Ships la guida è secca: *"Most worlds don't need this."* Sulle Creature: *"Add Creatures last — it's the most involved subsystem."*

Una cosa però la segnalo, perché potrebbe essere un residuo di una pianificazione diversa: nel tuo progetto ci sono `Creature.md`, `Mob.md` e soprattutto `Move.md` (le "Move" sono un concetto specifico del sistema creature). Sono tutti vuoti. Erano pensati per il creature-catcher, o li usavi semplicemente come bestiario/categorie di lore? Perché se è la seconda, il nome "Move" rischia di confonderti dopo — e vale la pena rinominarlo prima di popolarlo.

content.text:
963	## RPG Stats & Blueprints
   964	
   965	### RPG Stats and Blueprints
   966	
   967	This chapter covers three foundational pieces of any RPG-capable world: turning on the gameplay features you need, configuring your stat system, and building the species, occupation, and trait blueprints that give characters mechanical identity at character creation.
   968	
   969	### Enabling the RPG Features You Want
   970	
   971	Where: World Editor → Simulation tab → World Features section.
   972	
   973	Before any gameplay system exists in your world, you have to switch it on. Each toggle below enables a subsystem and reveals its corresponding editor. Nothing turns on automatically — you control exactly which systems your world uses.
   974	
   975	### Feature flag What it does
   976	
   977	Inventory Players can carry items, equip them, and use them. Adds the Inventory tab to the chat sidebar.
   978	Currency Enables money. Required for marketplaces. Adds currency balances to the inventory display.
   979	RPG Stats Enables stat-based mechanics — SPECIAL stats (or your custom stat system), species, occupations, traits. Adds the Stats tab to the chat sidebar.
   980	Combat Enables battle mode and the Director's combat tools. Combat surfaces through chat narration, with stat changes reflected in the Stats tab.
   981	Ships Enables vehicles that can travel between worlds. Most worlds don't need this.
   982	Creatures Enables the creature-catcher system — party of creatures, dex, encounters, evolution, moves. Adds the Creatures tab to the chat sidebar.
   983	Show Party Stats Includes party HP/MP/stats in the AI prompt so the AI knows how injured or exhausted everyone is.
   984	Recommendation for new RPG worlds: Start with Inventory and Currency. Add RPG Stats once you have a clear sense of your stat system. Add Creatures last — it's the most involved subsystem and builds on everything else.
   985	
   986	### Setting Up Your Stat System
   987	
   988	Where: World Editor → Simulation tab → Stat Config section.
   989	
   990	If you've enabled RPG Stats, this section is where you decide what stats your world uses. The default is SPECIAL: Strength, Perception, Endurance, Charisma, Intelligence, Agility, Luck. Most worlds can ship with these defaults and never look back.
   991	
   992	If you want a different system — D&D's six stats, a four-stat magic setup, something you invented — you can fully customize every part of it:
   993	
   994	| Field                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | What it does                                                                                                                                                                       |
   995	| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   996	| Stats                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | The list of stats. Each has an ID, a label, an abbreviation, a description, and an enabled toggle. Disable the SPECIAL stats you don't want, and add your own.                     |
   997	| Allocation Method                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | How players assign stats during character creation (see below).                                                                                                                    |
   998	| Base                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | Value / Max Value / Point Budget Numbers used for point-buy. Defaults: base 3, max 8, 21 points to spend.                                                                          |
   999	| HP                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | Label / MP Label What you call "HP" and "MP" in this world. "Vigor" and "Mana" are common alternatives.                                                                            |
  1000	| Stat Roles                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Which stat drives which combat behavior. By default, HP comes from Endurance, MP from Intelligence, physical attack from Strength, and so on. Remap these to match your stat list. |
  1001	| Vital Labels                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | Threshold-based display labels for HP and MP — e.g., below 25% shows as "Critical" instead of a bare number.                                                                       |
  1002	| Stat Value Labels                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | Threshold-based labels for any stat — e.g., a Strength of 6 shows as "high" instead of "6."                                                                                        |
  1003	| Species / Occupations / Traits Enabled Toggles for the three blueprint systems described in the next section.                                                                                                                                                                                                      |                                                                                                                                                                                    |
  1004	| Allocation                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Method                                                                                                                                                                             |
  1005	| Method                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | How it works                                                                                                                                                                       |
  1006	| Point Buy                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Default. Players spend a pool of points (21 by default) to raise stats from the base value (3) up to the max (8). Every point spent raises one stat by one.                        |
  1007	| Fixed                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Every character starts with the same preset values. Good for worlds where all players are on equal footing with no customization.                                                  |
  1008	| Free Assign                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | Players can put any number in any stat, unconstrained.                                                                                                                             |
  1009	| Roll                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | Stats are rolled with dice.                                                                                                                                                        |
  1010	| Why Stat                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | Roles matter                                                                                                                                                                       |
  1011	| The combat engine doesn't know what "Strength" means by name. It knows that a physical attack check uses whatever stat you've mapped to the physical attack role. By default that's Strength, but if your world uses "Brawn" and "Finesse" instead, you remap the physical attack role to whichever of those fits. |                                                                                                                                                                                    |
  1012	
  1013	This is what lets you build a fully custom stat system and still have combat work correctly out of the box. Roles are the bridge between your world's vocabulary and the underlying math.
  1014	
  1015	The available roles cover: HP scaling, MP scaling, physical attack, magic attack, physical defense, magic defense, speed (turn order), and accuracy.
  1016	
  1017	### Stat Value Labels
  1018	
  1019	If you set labels at thresholds — say, 0 = "poor," 3 = "average," 6 = "high," 8 = "exceptional" — the AI sees Strength: high in its prompt rather than Strength: 6. This is a display and AI-context choice. The number is still the number internally; it just gets translated into a word the AI can write around more naturally.
  1020	
  1021	You can leave this empty and let numbers speak for themselves. Labels work best in worlds where you want the AI to describe characters in qualitative terms rather than mechanical ones.
  1022	
  1023	### Species, Occupations, and Traits (Blueprints)
  1024	
  1025	Where: World Editor → RPG tab.
  1026	
  1027	These are the three character-creation building blocks. A player picks one species, one occupation, and any number of traits when they create their character — or you assign them when setting up an NPC. Each blueprint adjusts the character's base stats and carries flavor text the AI uses when writing that character.
  1028	
  1029	All three systems are optional and can be enabled or disabled independently in your Stat Config settings.
  1030	
  1031	### Species
  1032	
  1033	Species are biological or origin-based templates: Elf, Dwarf, Robot, Cybered Human, Forest Elemental. Each species has:
  1034	
  1035	Name and description — shown to the player during character creation and included in the AI's context.
  1036	Stat modifiers — additive bonuses or penalties applied to base stats (e.g., Elf: +1 Agility, −1 Endurance).
  1037	Avatar — optional image shown in the picker UI.
  1038	If your world has no biological variety — everyone is the same species — just don't create any. The blueprint system is entirely opt-in. An empty species list means character creation skips the species step.
  1039	
  1040	### Occupations
  1041	
  1042	Occupations are class or profession archetypes: Warrior, Merchant, Spellblade, Hacker, Wanderer. Same fields as species — name, description, stat modifiers, avatar. A character has exactly one occupation.
  1043	
  1044	Occupations are a good place to encode the mechanical identity of different playstyles. A Warrior might get +2 Strength and +1 Endurance; a Scholar might get +2 Intelligence and +1 Perception. The AI also uses the occupation description when narrating the character's actions, so write it in a way that communicates both the stat identity and the narrative flavor.
  1045	
  1046	### Traits
  1047	
  1048	Traits are smaller modifiers a character can stack: "Quick Reflexes," "Thick Skinned," "Silver-Tongued," "Lucky." Same fields — name, description, stat modifiers. A character can have many traits simultaneously.
  1049	
  1050	Traits are good for:
  1051	
  1052	### Fine-tuning a build after species and occupation are set
  1053	
  1054	### Representing injuries, blessings, or permanent conditions
  1055	Adding narrative texture without forcing a full class change
  1056	Giving NPCs distinguishing mechanical details without overbuilding their sheets
  1057	How modifiers stack
  1058	When the system computes a character's effective stats, it adds everything together:
  1059	
  1060	### base stats
  1061	
  1062	- species modifiers
  1063	- occupation modifiers
  1064	- sum of all trait modifiers
  1065	  Equipment modifiers (from equipped items) and active status effects layer on top of that. So if you give Elves +1 Agility, the Rogue occupation +1 Agility, and the "Cat-Quick" trait +1 Agility, a Cat-Quick Elven Rogue has +3 Agility before any gear or buffs. That's the intended design — blueprints are additive by default, and players (or you) choose how far to stack them.
  1066	
  1067	There is no diminishing returns or cap at the blueprint level. If you want stat caps, set them via the Max Value field in your Stat Config.
  1068	
  1069	### What comes next
  1070	
  1071	With features enabled, stats configured, and blueprints defined, your world has its mechanical skeleton. The next chapters cover building out the economy (currencies and marketplaces), the item lexicon, and creature systems — all of which build on the stat foundation you've laid here.
  1072	
  1073	---
  1074	
  1075	## Combat
[2595 lines total]

RPG Stats Enables stat-based mechanics — SPECIAL stats (or your custom stat system), species, occupations, traits. Adds the Stats tab to the chat sidebar.
Combat Enables battle mode and the Director's combat tools. Combat surfaces through chat narration, with stat changes reflected in the Stats tab.
Ships Enables vehicles that can travel between worlds. Most worlds don't need this.
Creatures Enables the creature-catcher system — party of creatures, dex, encounters, evolution, moves. Adds the Creatures tab to the chat sidebar.
Show Party Stats Includes party HP/MP/stats in the AI prompt so the AI knows how injured or exhausted everyone is.
Recommendation for new RPG worlds: Start with Inventory and Currency. Add RPG Stats once you have a clear sense of your stat system. Add Creatures last — it's the most involved subsystem and builds on everything else.

### Setting Up Your Stat System

Where: World Editor → Simulation tab → Stat Config section.

If you've enabled RPG Stats, this section is where you decide what stats your world uses. The default is SPECIAL: Strength, Perception, Endurance, Charisma, Intelligence, Agility, Luck. Most worlds can ship with these defaults and never look back.

If you want a different system — D&D's six stats, a four-stat magic setup, something you invented — you can fully customize every part of it:

| Field                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | What it does                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Stats                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | The list of stats. Each has an ID, a label, an abbreviation, a description, and an enabled toggle. Disable the SPECIAL stats you don't want, and add your own.                     |
| Allocation Method                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | How players assign stats during character creation (see below).                                                                                                                    |
| Base                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | Value / Max Value / Point Budget Numbers used for point-buy. Defaults: base 3, max 8, 21 points to spend.                                                                          |
| HP                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | Label / MP Label What you call "HP" and "MP" in this world. "Vigor" and "Mana" are common alternatives.                                                                            |
| Stat Roles                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Which stat drives which combat behavior. By default, HP comes from Endurance, MP from Intelligence, physical attack from Strength, and so on. Remap these to match your stat list. |
| Vital Labels                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | Threshold-based display labels for HP and MP — e.g., below 25% shows as "Critical" instead of a bare number.                                                                       |
| Stat Value Labels                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | Threshold-based labels for any stat — e.g., a Strength of 6 shows as "high" instead of "6."                                                                                        |
| Species / Occupations / Traits Enabled Toggles for the three blueprint systems described in the next section.                                                                                                                                                                                                      |                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Allocation                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Method                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Method                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | How it works                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Point Buy                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Default. Players spend a pool of points (21 by default) to raise stats from the base value (3) up to the max (8). Every point spent raises one stat by one.                        |
| Fixed                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Every character starts with the same preset values. Good for worlds where all players are on equal footing with no customization.                                                  |
| Free Assign                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | Players can put any number in any stat, unconstrained.                                                                                                                             |
| Roll                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | Stats are rolled with dice.                                                                                                                                                        |
| Why Stat                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | Roles matter                                                                                                                                                                       |
| The combat engine doesn't know what "Strength" means by name. It knows that a physical attack check uses whatever stat you've mapped to the physical attack role. By default that's Strength, but if your world uses "Brawn" and "Finesse" instead, you remap the physical attack role to whichever of those fits. |                                                                                                                                                                                    |

This is what lets you build a fully custom stat system and still have combat work correctly out of the box. Roles are the bridge between your world's vocabulary and the underlying math.

The available roles cover: HP scaling, MP scaling, physical attack, magic attack, physical defense, magic defense, speed (turn order), and accuracy.

### Stat Value Labels

If you set labels at thresholds — say, 0 = "poor," 3 = "average," 6 = "high," 8 = "exceptional" — the AI sees Strength: high in its prompt rather than Strength: 6. This is a display and AI-context choice. The number is still the number internally; it just gets translated into a word the AI can write around more naturally.

You can leave this empty and let numbers speak for themselves. Labels work best in worlds where you want the AI to describe characters in qualitative terms rather than mechanical ones.

### Species, Occupations, and Traits (Blueprints)

Where: World Editor → RPG tab.

These are the three character-creation building blocks. A player picks one species, one occupation, and any number of traits when they create their character — or you assign them when setting up an NPC. Each blueprint adjusts the character's base stats and carries flavor text the AI uses when writing that character.

All three systems are optional and can be enabled or disabled independently in your Stat Config settings.

### Species

Species are biological or origin-based templates: Elf, Dwarf, Robot, Cybered Human, Forest Elemental. Each species has:

Name and description — shown to the player during character creation and included in the AI's context.
Stat modifiers — additive bonuses or penalties applied to base stats (e.g., Elf: +1 Agility, −1 Endurance).
Avatar — optional image shown in the picker UI.
If your world has no biological variety — everyone is the same species — just don't create any. The blueprint system is entirely opt-in. An empty species list means character creation skips the species step.

### Occupations

Occupations are class or profession archetypes: Warrior, Merchant, Spellblade, Hacker, Wanderer. Same fields as species — name, description, stat modifiers, avatar. A character has exactly one occupation.

Occupations are a good place to encode the mechanical identity of different playstyles. A Warrior might get +2 Strength and +1 Endurance; a Scholar might get +2 Intelligence and +1 Perception. The AI also uses the occupation description when narrating the character's actions, so write it in a way that communicates both the stat identity and the narrative flavor.

### Traits

Traits are smaller modifiers a character can stack: "Quick Reflexes," "Thick Skinned," "Silver-Tongued," "Lucky." Same fields — name, description, stat modifiers. A character can have many traits simultaneously.

Traits are good for:

### Fine-tuning a build after species and occupation are set

### Representing injuries, blessings, or permanent conditions
Adding narrative texture without forcing a full class change
Giving NPCs distinguishing mechanical details without overbuilding their sheets
How modifiers stack
When the system computes a character's effective stats, it adds everything together:

### base stats

- species modifiers
- occupation modifiers
- sum of all trait modifiers
  Equipment modifiers (from equipped items) and active status effects layer on top of that. So if you give Elves +1 Agility, the Rogue occupation +1 Agility, and the "Cat-Quick" trait +1 Agility, a Cat-Quick Elven Rogue has +3 Agility before any gear or buffs. That's the intended design — blueprints are additive by default, and players (or you) choose how far to stack them.

There is no diminishing returns or cap at the blueprint level. If you want stat caps, set them via the Max Value field in your Stat Config.

### What comes next

With features enabled, stats configured, and blueprints defined, your world has its mechanical skeleton. The next chapters cover building out the economy (currencies and marketplaces), the item lexicon, and creature systems — all of which build on the stat foundation you've laid here.

---

1075	## Combat
  1076	
  1077	### Combat
  1078	
  1079	Combat in WyvernChat is an optional RPG layer — once you have stats enabled for your world, the Combat tab in the world editor lets you decide exactly how battles are resolved, narrated, and felt. This chapter walks through every authoring choice you'll face, explains what each one produces in play, and offers clear guidance on when to pick what.
  1080	
  1081	The Combat tab only appears after you enable RPG stats for your world. If you don't see it, visit your world's Settings or Simulation tab and turn on RPG stats first. See Chapter 7 — RPG Stats & Blueprints for how to set those up.
  1082	
  1083	If you never open the Combat tab, your world still runs fights using a solid set of defaults. Open it when you want battles to feel like your game — not a generic one.
  1084	
  1085	### Start with a preset
  1086	
  1087	The easiest way in is to click one of the preset buttons at the top of the tab. Each fills every setting with a coherent starting configuration. Tweak from there.
  1088	
  1089	Pokémon-style — stat-driven numeric combat: move power plus attacker stats versus defender stats, type effectiveness, critical hits. Designed for creature-catcher or monster-battler worlds where the math should track like a game.
  1090	D&D-style — dice-and-outcomes combat: each action rolls against a difficulty and lands on a tier (critical success, success, failure, or fumble), and the AI narrates that tier. Designed for adventure and tabletop-flavored worlds where drama matters more than arithmetic.
  1091	Fallout / VATS — coming soon; currently disabled.
  1092	You can change any individual setting after applying a preset — presets are a starting point, not a lock-in.
  1093	
  1094	The central choice: how is an attack decided?
  1095	The Combat Style setting is the most important decision you'll make. It controls the fundamental resolution mechanic for every attack in your world.
  1096	
  1097	### Storyteller (dice and outcomes)
  1098	
  1099	Every action rolls against a difficulty and lands somewhere on a four-tier scale: critical success, success, failure, or fumble. The AI is told which tier landed and narrates accordingly — a desperate swing that finds a gap in the armor, a glancing blow that barely connects, a humiliating stumble.
  1100	
  1101	Choose Storyteller when:
  1102	
  1103	Combat is about drama, tension, and cinematic description.
  1104	You're building an adventure world, a dark fantasy, or a tabletop RPG setting.
  1105	You want the AI to have interpretive latitude in how it describes a fight.
  1106	You don't need the hit points to track like a video game.
  1107	
  1108	### Numbers (stats and damage)
  1109	
  1110	Attacks use a real damage formula — move power, attacker stats, defender stats, type effectiveness, hit chance, and critical hit chance all feed into a numeric result. The AI is not told the number; it receives a description of the result (a heavy hit, a glancing blow, super effective, missed) and narrates from there.
  1111	
  1112	Choose Numbers when:
  1113	
  1114	You're building a creature-catcher, monster-battle, or competitive-style world.
  1115	You want fights to "add up" — where a tankier creature genuinely survives longer and a faster one genuinely moves first.
  1116	Players should feel like the system has real rules underneath.
  1117	Your moves have power values and your type chart is configured.
  1118	
  1119	### Mixing the two
  1120	
  1121	The toggle "Use different rules for creatures vs characters" lets you run both styles in the same world. The classic use case is a Pokémon-inspired world: creature-versus-creature battles use Numbers (full stat math), while human-character duels use Storyteller dice. Turn the toggle off to apply one style to everything.
  1122	
  1123	### Telling the engine what your stats mean (Role Mapping)
  1124	
  1125	Your world's stats can be named anything — HP, Vitality, Endurance, Grit, whatever fits your setting. Combat doesn't care about names; it cares about roles. The role-mapping dropdowns let you point each combat role at whichever of your stats fills that function:
  1126	
  1127	Attack power — the stat that makes hits harder (your Attack, Strength, Magic Power, etc.)
  1128	Defense / damage soak — the stat that reduces incoming hits (your Defense, Toughness, Armor, etc.)
  1129	Initiative / turn order — the stat that determines who acts first (your Speed, Agility, Reflex, etc.)
  1130	Health pool — the stat that scales maximum HP (your HP, Endurance, Constitution, etc.)
  1131	Once mapped, every formula in the system uses the right stat automatically. This is what allows a Pokémon world and a gritty swords-and-sorcery world to both work without touching any underlying code.
  1132	
  1133	Role mapping also appears in the Simulation tab — it is the same setting. Edit it in either place.
  1134	
  1135	### Health and energy pools
  1136	
  1137	Here you set how large health and energy (MP/stamina) pools are:
  1138	
  1139	Base amount — the minimum HP or energy any character starts with, independent of stats.
  1140	Per stat-point growth — how much each point of the health or energy stat adds to the pool. Higher means stats matter more; lower means everyone's closer to the same baseline.
  1141	Per level growth — how much HP or energy increases each time a character gains a level.
  1142	Tuning these together determines the pace of combat. High base + high per-level = long, attrition-heavy fights. Low base + low growth = fast and lethal. There's a matching set of controls for the energy pool if your world uses one to power special moves.
  1143	
  1144	### Turn order
  1145	
  1146	Also configured here: who acts when.
  1147	
  1148	By stat — the character with the higher initiative stat always acts first each round. Predictable, tactical.
  1149	By roll — each character rolls for initiative each round. Swingier; anyone can go first.
  1150	Simultaneous — all characters act at the same time, no turn order. Works best for free-form or narrative-forward combat.
  1151	
  1152	### Numbers-style settings
  1153	
  1154	These controls only appear when you've chosen Numbers as your combat style. They let you tune the formula.
  1155	
  1156	### Damage style
  1157	
  1158	How raw damage is calculated before it reaches the target:
  1159	
  1160	Power + attack − defense — a straightforward additive formula. High-attack characters deal reliably high damage; high-defense targets reduce it consistently. Familiar to players of classic JRPGs.
  1161	Ratio (attacker vs. defender stats, Pokémon-like) — damage scales with how much the attacker's stat outpaces the defender's, optionally amplified by level. A strong attacker versus a weak defender does much more damage than the stat difference would suggest linearly; a close matchup produces modest results. Best for creature-battle worlds.
  1162	Fixed-power move — the move has a set base damage; the target's defense softens the blow but cannot fully block it. Useful for special attacks or abilities that should always deal meaningful damage.
  1163	
  1164	### Accuracy
  1165	
  1166	Always hit — attacks never miss. Simpler; removes a frustration point.
  1167	Roll against the move's hit chance — moves can miss, creating moments of relief or tension. Requires your moves to have hit-chance values configured.
  1168	
  1169	### Critical hits
  1170	
  1171	Set the crit rate (how often a critical hit occurs) and the crit multiplier (how much extra damage it deals). The AI is told a crit landed but never sees the multiplier — it narrates something appropriately dramatic.
  1172	
  1173	### Type effectiveness
  1174	
  1175	When enabled, the type chart you've configured for your world applies to every hit. Moves can be super effective, resisted, or completely immune, and the AI is told the effectiveness tier so it can reflect it in description (a devastating strike, an ineffective blow, completely blocked).
  1176	
  1177	For type effectiveness to work, your moves need type values and your world's type chart needs to be configured. See Chapter 10 — Creatures, Moves, Natures & Abilities for how to set that up.
  1178	
  1179	### Storyteller-style settings
  1180	
  1181	These controls only appear when you've chosen Storyteller as your combat style.
  1182	
  1183	Base difficulty — how hard a typical action is to land on the four-tier scale. Raise it to make combat grimmer and more punishing; lower it for heroic, action-forward play.
  1184	Attack modifier stat / defense modifier stat — which of your stats shifts the attack roll up or down, and which raises the difficulty the attacker is rolling against.
  1185	Critical margin — how far above the difficulty threshold counts as a critical success, and how far below counts as a fumble. A small margin makes crits and fumbles common; a large margin makes them memorable exceptions.
  1186	
  1187	### Battle Mode: what the AI sees during a fight
  1188	
  1189	While a battle is active, the AI receives a short briefing alongside the normal world context. The Battle Mode section lets you write and frame that briefing.
  1190	
  1191	Label — the heading for the battle briefing block in the prompt (e.g. "Active Battle," "Pokémon Battle," "Encounter"). Defaults to something sensible if left blank.
  1192	Battle instructions — guidance for how the AI should narrate combat: the tone, pacing, and style you want. Leave this blank to use the system default. Add it when you want something specific — visceral and punishing, lighthearted and energetic, coldly tactical.
  1193	Wrapper tags — optionally wrap the battle briefing in opening and closing tags (for example <Battle> / </Battle>) instead of a plain label heading. Use this if your world's prompts use a tagged structure and you want combat to match.
  1194	Show enemy health — tells the AI whether the opponent is fresh, hurt, badly hurt, or on the verge of collapse. On by default. Turn it off if you prefer the AI to infer enemy condition from the fight's history rather than having it stated outright.
  1195	
  1196	### How combat reads in play
  1197	
  1198	A few things that are worth understanding as a creator, because they shape how your tuning choices land:
  1199	
  1200	The AI never sees raw numbers. The engine translates every numeric result into language before the AI reads it: "a heavy hit," "the foe is badly hurt," "super effective," "a glancing blow." This means the AI narrates mood and drama, not arithmetic. The underlying numbers are tracked accurately behind the scenes — they just stay there.
  1201	
  1202	The story reflects what actually happened. When a player uses a battle action, the real resolved outcome (the hit that connected, the miss, the capture that worked) is fed into the AI's briefing so its narration matches what actually occurred — not a guess, not an improvisation.
  1203	
  1204	Players can expand the details. Every battle message includes an Actions strip players can open to see the actual rolls, damage values, and step-by-step results. This is visible to players, not part of the AI briefing.
  1205	
  1206	Rerolls stay consistent. If a player swipes or regenerates a battle reply, the resolved outcome stays the same — the new narration describes the same hit, the same miss, the same result, just written differently.
  1207	
  1208	### Quick recipes
  1209	
  1210	### "I want Pokémon-style creature battles."
  1211	Click the Pokémon-style preset. Map your creature stats to the Attack, Defense, Speed, and HP roles. Make sure your creature moves have power values and types, and configure your type chart. Enable type effectiveness in the Numbers settings. Done.
  1212	
  1213	### "I want classic tabletop adventure combat."
  1214	
  1215	Click the D&D-style preset. Map your stats to the appropriate roles. Optionally raise the health base and per-level growth to give characters more room to breathe across a long encounter.
  1216	
  1217	"I want Pokémon battles for creatures but narrative duels for human characters."
  1218	Click Pokémon-style. Turn on "Use different rules for creatures vs characters." Set the character-specific combat style to Storyteller. Configure both sets of stat role mappings.
  1219	
  1220	### "I want fast, lethal fights with no misses."
  1221	
  1222	Choose Numbers. Set accuracy to always hit. Lower the base HP and per-level growth so fights end in a few exchanges. Crit rate is optional flavor.
  1223	
  1224	### "I want heroic high-fantasy combat where the heroes usually succeed."
  1225	
  1226	Choose Storyteller. Set a lower base difficulty. Set a small critical margin so strong rolls land as crits often. Describe the style you want in the battle instructions — something that biases the narration toward momentum and triumph.
  1227	
  1228	---
  1229	
  1230	## Items, Currencies, and Markets

{"language": "markdown", "code": "## Combat

### Combat

Combat in WyvernChat is an optional RPG layer — once you have stats enabled for your world, the Combat tab in the world editor lets you decide exactly how battles are resolved, narrated, and felt. This chapter walks through every authoring choice you'll face, explains what each one produces in play, and offers clear guidance on when to pick what.

The Combat tab only appears after you enable RPG stats for your world. If you don't see it, visit your world's Settings or Simulation tab and turn on RPG stats first. See Chapter 7 — RPG Stats & Blueprints for how to set those up.

If you never open the Combat tab, your world still runs fights using a solid set of defaults. Open it when you want battles to feel like your game — not a generic one.

### Start with a preset

The easiest way in is to click one of the preset buttons at the top of the tab. Each fills every setting with a coherent starting configuration. Tweak from there.

Pokémon-style — stat-driven numeric combat: move power plus attacker stats versus defender stats, type effectiveness, critical hits. Designed for creature-catcher or monster-battler worlds where the math should track like a game.
D&D-style — dice-and-outcomes combat: each action rolls against a difficulty and lands on a tier (critical success, success, failure, or fumble), and the AI narrates that tier. Designed for adventure and tabletop-flavored worlds where drama matters more than arithmetic.
Fallout / VATS — coming soon; currently disabled.
You can change any individual setting after applying a preset — presets are a starting point, not a lock-in.

The central choice: how is an attack decided?
The Combat Style setting is the most important decision you'll make. It controls the fundamental resolution mechanic for every attack in your world.

### Storyteller (dice and outcomes)

Every action rolls against a difficulty and lands somewhere on a four-tier scale: critical success, success, failure, or fumble. The AI is told which tier landed and narrates accordingly — a desperate swing that finds a gap in the armor, a glancing blow that barely connects, a humiliating stumble.

Choose Storyteller when:

Combat is about drama, tension, and cinematic description.
You're building an adventure world, a dark fantasy, or a tabletop RPG setting.
You want the AI to have interpretive latitude in how it describes a fight.
You don't need the hit points to track like a video game.

### Numbers (stats and damage)

Attacks use a real damage formula — move power, attacker stats, defender stats, type effectiveness, hit chance, and critical hit chance all feed into a numeric result. The AI is not told the number; it receives a description of the result (a heavy hit, a glancing blow, super effective, missed) and narrates from there.

Choose Numbers when:

You're building a creature-catcher, monster-battle, or competitive-style world.
You want fights to "add up" — where a tankier creature genuinely survives longer and a faster one genuinely moves first.
Players should feel like the system has real rules underneath.
Your moves have power values and your type chart is configured.

### Mixing the two

The toggle "Use different rules for creatures vs characters" lets you run both styles in the same world. The classic use case is a Pokémon-inspired world: creature-versus-creature battles use Numbers (full stat math), while human-character duels use Storyteller dice. Turn the toggle off to apply one style to everything.

### Telling the engine what your stats mean (Role Mapping)

Your world's stats can be named anything — HP, Vitality, Endurance, Grit, whatever fits your setting. Combat doesn't care about names; it cares about roles. The role-mapping dropdowns let you point each combat role at whichever of your stats fills that function:

Attack power — the stat that makes hits harder (your Attack, Strength, Magic Power, etc.)
Defense / damage soak — the stat that reduces incoming hits (your Defense, Toughness, Armor, etc.)
Initiative / turn order — the stat that determines who acts first (your Speed, Agility, Reflex, etc.)
Health pool — the stat that scales maximum HP (your HP, Endurance, Constitution, etc.)
Once mapped, every formula in the system uses the right stat automatically. This is what allows a Pokémon world and a gritty swords-and-sorcery world to both work without touching any underlying code.

Role mapping also appears in the Simulation tab — it is the same setting. Edit it in either place.

### Health and energy pools

Here you set how large health and energy (MP/stamina) pools are:

Base amount — the minimum HP or energy any character starts with, independent of stats.
Per stat-point growth — how much each point of the health or energy stat adds to the pool. Higher means stats matter more; lower means everyone's closer to the same baseline.
Per level growth — how much HP or energy increases each time a character gains a level.
Tuning these together determines the pace of combat. High base + high per-level = long, attrition-heavy fights. Low base + low growth = fast and lethal. There's a matching set of controls for the energy pool if your world uses one to power special moves.

### Turn order

Also configured here: who acts when.

By stat — the character with the higher initiative stat always acts first each round. Predictable, tactical.
By roll — each character rolls for initiative each round. Swingier; anyone can go first.
Simultaneous — all characters act at the same time, no turn order. Works best for free-form or narrative-forward combat.

### Numbers-style settings

These controls only appear when you've chosen Numbers as your combat style. They let you tune the formula.

### Damage style

How raw damage is calculated before it reaches the target:

Power + attack − defense — a straightforward additive formula. High-attack characters deal reliably high damage; high-defense targets reduce it consistently. Familiar to players of classic JRPGs.
Ratio (attacker vs. defender stats, Pokémon-like) — damage scales with how much the attacker's stat outpaces the defender's, optionally amplified by level. A strong attacker versus a weak defender does much more damage than the stat difference would suggest linearly; a close matchup produces modest results. Best for creature-battle worlds.
Fixed-power move — the move has a set base damage; the target's defense softens the blow but cannot fully block it. Useful for special attacks or abilities that should always deal meaningful damage.

### Accuracy

Always hit — attacks never miss. Simpler; removes a frustration point.
Roll against the move's hit chance — moves can miss, creating moments of relief or tension. Requires your moves to have hit-chance values configured.

### Critical hits

Set the crit rate (how often a critical hit occurs) and the crit multiplier (how much extra damage it deals). The AI is told a crit landed but never sees the multiplier — it narrates something appropriately dramatic.

### Type effectiveness

When enabled, the type chart you've configured for your world applies to every hit. Moves can be super effective, resisted, or completely immune, and the AI is told the effectiveness tier so it can reflect it in description (a devastating strike, an ineffective blow, completely blocked).

For type effectiveness to work, your moves need type values and your world's type chart needs to be configured. See Chapter 10 — Creatures, Moves, Natures & Abilities for how to set that up.

### Storyteller-style settings

These controls only appear when you've chosen Storyteller as your combat style.

Base difficulty — how hard a typical action is to land on the four-tier scale. Raise it to make combat grimmer and more punishing; lower it for heroic, action-forward play.
Attack modifier stat / defense modifier stat — which of your stats shifts the attack roll up or down, and which raises the difficulty the attacker is rolling against.
Critical margin — how far above the difficulty threshold counts as a critical success, and how far below counts as a fumble. A small margin makes crits and fumbles common; a large margin makes them memorable exceptions.

### Battle Mode: what the AI sees during a fight

While a battle is active, the AI receives a short briefing alongside the normal world context. The Battle Mode section lets you write and frame that briefing.

Label — the heading for the battle briefing block in the prompt (e.g. "Active Battle," "Pokémon Battle," "Encounter"). Defaults to something sensible if left blank.
Battle instructions — guidance for how the AI should narrate combat: the tone, pacing, and style you want. Leave this blank to use the system default. Add it when you want something specific — visceral and punishing, lighthearted and energetic, coldly tactical.
Wrapper tags — optionally wrap the battle briefing in opening and closing tags (for example <Battle> / </Battle>) instead of a plain label heading. Use this if your world's prompts use a tagged structure and you want combat to match.
Show enemy health — tells the AI whether the opponent is fresh, hurt, badly hurt, or on the verge of collapse. On by default. Turn it off if you prefer the AI to infer enemy condition from the fight's history rather than having it stated outright.

### How combat reads in play

A few things that are worth understanding as a creator, because they shape how your tuning choices land:

The AI never sees raw numbers. The engine translates every numeric result into language before the AI reads it: "a heavy hit," "the foe is badly hurt," "super effective," "a glancing blow." This means the AI narrates mood and drama, not arithmetic. The underlying numbers are tracked accurately behind the scenes — they just stay there.

The story reflects what actually happened. When a player uses a battle action, the real resolved outcome (the hit that connected, the miss, the capture that worked) is fed into the AI's briefing so its narration matches what actually occurred — not a guess, not an improvisation.

Players can expand the details. Every battle message includes an Actions strip players can open to see the actual rolls, damage values, and step-by-step results. This is visible to players, not part of the AI briefing.

Rerolls stay consistent. If a player swipes or regenerates a battle reply, the resolved outcome stays the same — the new narration describes the same hit, the same miss, the same result, just written differently.

### Quick recipes

### "I want Pokémon-style creature battles."
Click the Pokémon-style preset. Map your creature stats to the Attack, Defense, Speed, and HP roles. Make sure your creature moves have power values and types, and configure your type chart. Enable type effectiveness in the Numbers settings. Done.

### "I want classic tabletop adventure combat."

Click the D&D-style preset. Map your stats to the appropriate roles. Optionally raise the health base and per-level growth to give characters more room to breathe across a long encounter.

"I want Pokémon battles for creatures but narrative duels for human characters."
Click Pokémon-style. Turn on "Use different rules for creatures vs characters." Set the character-specific combat style to Storyteller. Configure both sets of stat role mappings.

### "I want fast, lethal fights with no misses."

Choose Numbers. Set accuracy to always hit. Lower the base HP and per-level growth so fights end in a few exchanges. Crit rate is optional flavor.

### "I want heroic high-fantasy combat where the heroes usually succeed."

Choose Storyteller. Set a lower base difficulty. Set a small critical margin so strong rolls land as crits often. Describe the style you want in the battle instructions — something that biases the narration toward momentum and triumph.
